000c7f50-ff95-5a24-b26f-2c2401107ffd.name: *Mosque of the Sultan, Cairo*
000c7f50-ff95-5a24-b26f-2c2401107ffd.dimensions: Height: 161 mm photograph, Width: 210 mm photograph
000c7f50-ff95-5a24-b26f-2c2401107ffd.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
000c7f50-ff95-5a24-b26f-2c2401107ffd.keywords: Albumen process; Grand Tour; Holy Land; Victorian; Egypt; travel; history of photography
000c7f50-ff95-5a24-b26f-2c2401107ffd.description2:
During the 1850s and 1860s, Francis Frith was one of England's most celebrated photographers. In September 1856, he set sail for Alexandria. This was the first of three trips that Frith would take to the Near East. The model was that of the 'Grand Tour'.  
Any analysis of Frith's work leads to the discourse of the tension between empirical knowledge and spiritual awareness in Victorian England. The photograph operated as a tool that could have moral influence upon those who viewed them with their ability to bring viewers to the locations of holy events.  
But even from a purely secular point of view, Frith's photographs become operators within an ideology specific to the era. Frith's thematic choices are manifest of the Victorians' tendency to regard themselves in relation to the larger history of mankind.

001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.name: Garden Mosque
001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.holder: Baden-Württemberg Castles and Gardens, State Agency for Property Assets and Construction
001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.dates: The mosque complex comprises a cloister-like colonnade in the east (1779–84) and a main building (1782–86) flanked by two minarets (1786–95) in the west
001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.author: Hartmut Troll
001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.history:
The mosque in the Schwetzingen palace gardens today is the last surviving example of a type of building quite common in European landscape gardens up to the end of the 18th-century.  
The mosque, built 1782–95 by Nicolas de Pigage, was preceded by the Ambulatory, designed inside a Turkish Garden, which was first mentioned in 1774. Work on the actual mosque building started after Elector Carl Theodor had moved to Munich. The Ambulatory itself already represents contemporaneous ideas of what a mosque building looked like; the similarities with the feature of the holy sites of Mecca, published by Fischer von Erlach, are as unmistakable as the similarity of the corner pavilions with the mosque built by Chambers at Kew Gardens. The mosque itself is a fairly autonomous structure with a temple-like portico and Baroque dome.
001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.keywords: Garden Building; Turkish garden; Arabic inscriptions; minarets; Mosque; Moorish style; Romanticism; gardens
001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.description2: The mosque is surrounded by a “Turkish garden” with winding paths and exotic plants. The architectural feature of the central building provides an original variation on the language of shapes found in baroque churches. Quotations from the western architectural history are combined with oriental motifs and inscriptions from the Qur'an. The minarets are positioned slightly in front of the western façade. The colonnade walkway with its rectangular layout is comprised of latticework open on all sides. The octagonal pavilions are decorated with dictums in Arabic and German. One striking feature is the refined roofscape with different basic slatecovered shapes, adorned by innumerable gilded crescents. The mosque’s interior is comprised of a round central hall, richly and colourfully decorated. Various general maxims are inscribed in Arabic and translated into German. These texts are not religious in nature, but generally invoke virtues, such as wisdom, diligence and discretion.

0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.name: Italian Company Breda Ernesto. Factory for Torpedoes and Navy Equipment, Milan. View of the Female Section of Lathes Division. Production of 75 mm Shrapnel Shells
0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.author: Cristina Mosillo, Giulia Barrera
0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.archival: ACS, Ministero armi e munizioni, Ufficio storiografico della mobilitazione civile e industriale, Archivio fotografico, fasc. 148, foto 2039, neg. 2195 B.
0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.third_name: Soc. Italiana Breda Ernesto. Stabilimento per siluri e lavori di marina, Milano. Veduta  del reparto femminile della torneria. Lavorazione degli shrapnels da 75 mm.
0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.second_name: Women working in a factory that produced military equipment, during World War I
0066daed-f170-56db-b502-467e8b3e136c.description2:
Women working at lathes to make shrapnel shells in an Italian factory that produced torpedoes and other weapons. The war had an important impact on women’s work.  
As historian Perry Willson pointed out, during WWI “women rarely directly substituted for men, instead tending to move into new work roles produced by wartime expansion.”  
In Italy, the number of women who worked in factories producing weapons and ammunitions rose from 23,000 in 1915 to 198,000 in 1918. The numbers were far less than the women who participated in war production with more traditional “female roles”, such as making uniforms (400,000) or knitting woollen garments for the soldiers (200,000). However, Willson explained, women working in weapons’ factories had a relevance “as symbolic harbinger of change that greatly outweighed their actual numbers.”

en: Willson, Perry R., *Women in Twentieth-century Italy*, New York: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010.

007d6f6b-4f84-5cd4-97d4-b1637e409355.name: Emigrant family

007d6f6b-4f84-5cd4-97d4-b1637e409355.description2: The 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey was based upon religious identity, and involved the Greek Orthodox citizens of Turkey and the Muslim citizens of Greece. The "Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations" was signed at Lausanne, Switzerland, on 30 January 1923, by the governments of Greece and Turkey. This photo belongs to a Turkish family who migrated from Crete to Turkey in 1925.

00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.name: Constitution of the Slav-Macedonian Scientific and Literary Society in Saint Petersburg
00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.holder: University of St. Cyril and Methodius - Publisher
00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.archival: Documents on the Struggle of the Macedonian People for Independence and a Nation-State, Vol. I, Skopje, 1985
00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.description2: The Slav-Macedonian Scientific Literary Society was established in St. Petersburg on 16 December 1903, acting under the patronage of the St. Petersburg Slav Charitable Society. Its founders were Krste Petkov Misirkov (1874–1926) and Dimitija Chupovski, who worked actively on the recognition of Macedonian as distinct Slavic language and the opening of native-language schools for children in Macedonia. The Society, also known as the Macedonian Colony in St. Petersburg, gathered many distinguished Macedonian writers, poets and publicists. Its extensive scientific and literary activities have brought about explicit formulation of the Macedonian national program. The Society largely contributed to issuing a periodical publication in Macedonian and Russian language called “Makedonski Golos” (“Macedonian Voice"). It played an important role in the national awakening of Macedonians and bringing forth the issue of the Macedonian autonomy in the international community.

00c2f038-d775-56aa-a8e0-bba81f9f6642.name: Façade of the Palace of Mushatta
00c2f038-d775-56aa-a8e0-bba81f9f6642.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
00c2f038-d775-56aa-a8e0-bba81f9f6642.dates: AD 743–744; given by the Ottoman sultan ‘Abd al-Hamid II to Emperor Wilhelm II in 1903
00c2f038-d775-56aa-a8e0-bba81f9f6642.author: Stefan Weber
00c2f038-d775-56aa-a8e0-bba81f9f6642.second_name: Decorative entrance facade of the Umayyad caliphal palace
00c2f038-d775-56aa-a8e0-bba81f9f6642.description2: The Umayyad palace façade of Mushatta – gifted by Ottoman sultan `Abd al-Hamid II – is one of the key works of Islamic art and a prime example of shared heritage. The monument shows the origins of a cultural era rooting in the various local traditions of Late Antiquity and also its early development. It hence became seminal for the Islamic art department, whose very establishment by Wilhelm von Bode in 1904 is due to this gift.

00c8cda2-d033-5a89-89e5-4f6a4483e3da.name: The Hijaz Railway construction workers
00c8cda2-d033-5a89-89e5-4f6a4483e3da.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
00c8cda2-d033-5a89-89e5-4f6a4483e3da.dates: Late 19th century – begining of the 20th century
00c8cda2-d033-5a89-89e5-4f6a4483e3da.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph The Hijaz Railways
00c8cda2-d033-5a89-89e5-4f6a4483e3da.description2: The Hijaz Railway was a narrow-gauge railway (1,050mm/3ft, 5 11⁄32 in track gauge) that ran from Damascus to Medina, through the Hijaz region of Saudi Arabia, with a branch line to Haifa on the Mediterranean Sea. It was a part of the Ottoman railway network and was built to extend the line from the Haydarpaşa Terminal in Istanbul beyond Damascus to the holy city of Mecca. It got no further than Medina, 400 kilometres (250mi) short of Mecca, due to the interruption of the construction works caused by the outbreak of World War I.

00dac457-85a0-5a63-aebd-676267b9816c.name: Société des Fermes Françaises de Tunisie
00dac457-85a0-5a63-aebd-676267b9816c.description2: French agriculture in Tunisia came about either through the establishment of large properties by private initiatives, or the arrangement of settlers by the public authorities. This is a text from the "first phase" - one of the "companies" (of "French farms") had purchased a large plot of land, and employed a number of (largely Arab and Italian) workers to cultivate it. It aims to publicise the company and make it attractive to both prospective immigrants to tunisia, and attract funds.

Silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom.

00eecee6-1a79-5ca4-885a-64eb797adc19.name: *The bas-reliefs of Trajan's Column, reproduced in electroplating and exhibited in a room of the new Louvre*
00eecee6-1a79-5ca4-885a-64eb797adc19.second_name: Taken from the collection *Topographie de Paris*, "1er arrondissement, 1er quartier, Le Louvre"
00eecee6-1a79-5ca4-885a-64eb797adc19.description2: Trajan's Column, erected in Rome, is famous for its exceptional bas-reliefs commemorating the victory of the Emperor over the Dacians. In 1861, with the aim of making it known to the French public, Napoléon III had the column moulded and a replica installed in Paris. This was achieved thanks to the new electroplating technique, and the copy was placed in the Musée du Louvre. However, in 1870 the column was judged too large, and was sent to the Château de Saint-Germain, where it was quickly installed in the moat. In this image shows visitors at the Louvre, examining the story reproduced by Trajan's Column.

01309821-1550-570d-b610-d7e90337db0f.name: Çırağan Palace
01309821-1550-570d-b610-d7e90337db0f.keywords: Photograph; Old İstanbul Photograph; İstanbul; Pascal Sebah
01309821-1550-570d-b610-d7e90337db0f.description2: Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. In 1857 he opened his first photography studio in Istanbul. Çırağan Palace, built by Sultan Abdülâziz, was designed by the palace architect Nigoğayos Balyan and constructed by his sons Sarkis and Hagop Balyan between 1863 and 1867. This was a period in which all Ottoman sultans used to build their own palaces rather than using those of their ancestors. Çırağan Palace is the last example of this period. The inner walls and the roof were made of wood, the outer walls of colourful marble. The palace is connected with a beautiful marble bridge to the Yıldız Palace on the hill behind. A very high garden wall protects the palace from the outer world.

01425452-ab97-5882-bfb1-7f4f896ba157.name: Omar Pasha (1806–1871)
01425452-ab97-5882-bfb1-7f4f896ba157.keywords: Omar Pasha; Croatia; Bosnia; Ottoman empire; Herzegovina
01425452-ab97-5882-bfb1-7f4f896ba157.description2: Portrait of Omar Pasha. He was born in Croatia in 1806 near the Turkish-Hungarian border. In 1828 he deserted from the Austrian army and joined the Ottoman administration in Bosnia. After a long career in the Ottoman army, he became the military governor of Bucharest and commanded the Ottoman forces at the siege of Sevastopol in Crimea. In 1862 he suppressed an uprising in Herzogovina and led a victorious campaign against Montenegro. In 1868 he became War Minister and died in 1871 in Istanbul.

01436bcc-073d-529a-9751-7349d0fd45fc.name: Wooden Qur’an Stand
01436bcc-073d-529a-9751-7349d0fd45fc.type: Hardwood Qur'an Stand with bone and mother-of-pearl inlay
01436bcc-073d-529a-9751-7349d0fd45fc.holder: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation / Sharjah Museums Department
01436bcc-073d-529a-9751-7349d0fd45fc.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
01436bcc-073d-529a-9751-7349d0fd45fc.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
01436bcc-073d-529a-9751-7349d0fd45fc.description2: Items like this Qur’an stand were popular props in Orientalist painting. On the inside, this hard wood Qur’an stand, which is inlaid with ebony, bone and mother-of-pearl, is decorated with two large square geometric panels, surrounded by a wide zig-zag border. The two squares are in turn subdivided into four small squares, filled with abstract star motifs. On the underside, the stand has two large geometric roundels. Two narrow, rectangular mashrabiyyah panels occupy the upper part of the feet. The remaining surfaces surrounding them are filled with chequerboard designs.

01438940-6e4b-5dae-9321-45c0f28c82d7.name: *The Aqueduct in the Forest of Belgrade, Istanbul*
01438940-6e4b-5dae-9321-45c0f28c82d7.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
01438940-6e4b-5dae-9321-45c0f28c82d7.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
01438940-6e4b-5dae-9321-45c0f28c82d7.description2: This painting by an anonymous Ottoman artist shows the aqueduct of Belgrade Forest outside Istanbul. Istanbul’s water was stored in the reservoirs of Belgrade Forest and conveyed to the city across a number of aqueducts like this one. Established in early Ottoman times, the Istanbul water supply system was expanded and improved throughout the Ottoman period, incorporating complex systems of reservoirs, aqueducts and supply pipes endling in fountains and waterspouts.

019530a6-cc5d-510e-8a02-0122394f5817.name: Revolver
019530a6-cc5d-510e-8a02-0122394f5817.description: The Lebel Revolver was the standard issue sidearm in the French military during the First World War, produced in Saint Etienne and used by the French army between 1892 and before 1924. The 1892 Model is a double/single action, six round cylinder revolver that fires 8-millimetre rounds. It was issued to officers in the French Army, Navy, and National Gendarmerie, amongst others. It is commonly called the Lebel Revolver after the gun designer Colonel Nicolas Lebel. For loading and releasing the empty cases, the chambers are accessed through swinging the cylinder to the right. Originally chambered for an 8mm gunpowder cartridge round, later models issued during World War I and thereafter fired the same 8mm cartridge loaded with smokeless powder. Serial number 21093.

01a64f5c-ceca-5e43-b3af-115b31492d64.name: Portrait of Abraham Salamon De Camondo
01a64f5c-ceca-5e43-b3af-115b31492d64.holder: The Quincentennial Foundation Museum, Zulfaris Synagogue Museum
01a64f5c-ceca-5e43-b3af-115b31492d64.description2: The Camondo Family is a family of Spanish-Portuguese Jewish origin. Abraham Salomon Camondo, who was born in İstanbul in 1781, acted as the Ottoman government's banker before the establishment of the Ottoman Bank. He founded a bank called "*Isaac et Compagnie Camondo*" with his brother Isaac in 1815. The bank grew in a short time period into a reputable international financial institution. Camondo prospered greatly and became the prime banker to the Ottoman Empire until the founding of the Imperial Ottoman Bank in 1863. The bank had a close relationship with the business community and banks of London, Paris and the Vienna Stock Exchange. The bank had also funded defence needs of Ottoman Empire during the Crimean War.

01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.name: Cup and a stand
01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.keywords: Political and diplomatic engagement; cup; stand; metalwork; domestic vessels
01b5fb2d-6f55-548b-abb2-c28971f1148f.description2: Dimitrija Chupovski (1878-1940) was a distinguished Macedonian intellectual who lived and worked in Russia. Being the President of the Slav-Macedonian Scientific Literary Society in St. Petersburg, he contributed to the publishing of historical memorandums and other official acts that presented the national ideology and objectives for unity and liberation of Macedonia. He also published numerous articles drawing attention to the partitioning of Macedonia after the Balkan Wars. In his struggle for preserving the integrity of Macedonia he wrote various memoranda to governments of western countries on many occasions.

01e7089c-8585-5199-92a7-c9b05620637b.name: [Paris] stock exchange
01e7089c-8585-5199-92a7-c9b05620637b.description2: This building (Palais Brongniart), located in the heart of Paris, housed the French stock exchange for almost two centuries. Its atmosphere, as a powerful financial building bearing witness to great bankers' fortunes and failures, inspired writers such as Honoré de Balzac in La Maison Nucingen and Émile Zola in L’Argent.

02125310-0cbe-5f6f-833f-c178410397b3.name: Official document regarding the connection of Beirut–Damascus railway line to Beirut Port

022636e4-0dfa-5ef8-9246-5b40c6f3adf2.description2: Bridal chest painted with gold paste on a coloured background, and a chiselled copper hinge.

025b84b0-d00d-5c21-a749-98f3596f9d77.name: Boots
025b84b0-d00d-5c21-a749-98f3596f9d77.description: Men’s leather riding boots. The applications of leather in different colours, with representation of geometric patterns, follow the customs and superstitions of the Hausa. The Hausa possessed, in every community, workshops for producing and dyeing articles of leather, though the most out-standing locations are those of Kano and Sokoto in Nigeria; places producing, since the medieval times, the thinnest skins used in Europe. The skins are those of goat, preferably of the males, and the dye receives the local name of *bagaruwa*. This product is usually processed by women, and it is also used for treating dysentery. The products of the Hausa are distributed, by trade, across wide zones of the Sahel and Subsaharian Africa.

02992f2b-3701-5bc3-ba32-d5f6226b56ef.name: Bowl (*Sakızlık*)
02992f2b-3701-5bc3-ba32-d5f6226b56ef.holder: Vehbi Koç Foundation Sadberk Hanim Museum
02992f2b-3701-5bc3-ba32-d5f6226b56ef.keywords: minor arts, applied arts, silver objects
02992f2b-3701-5bc3-ba32-d5f6226b56ef.description2: From historical sources, we learn that vessels made of gold and silver were widely used in the Ottoman palace. Starting from the end of the 18th century, Baroque and Rococo forms of Western style replaced classical Ottoman designs. We find roses in relief, the Ottoman coat-of-arms, architectural compositions, casted flowers, birds and animals on a multitude of the vessels of the era. This cylindrical cup with pedestal foot and cupola-like hinged lid was made of vermeil silver. On the body of the cup we see a floral pattern and hanging lambs placed alternatingly. Flowers, buds and leaves are made from rubies and diamonds nailed into gold and silver contours. On the lid – instead of lamb motif on the body – a chalice was used. The foot of the chalice is in the form of a cherub from which a bundle of rays projects.

02aa485b-b3bc-53cc-91c5-b9f267c8d3b1.name: *Constantinople et le Bosphore de Thrace*
02aa485b-b3bc-53cc-91c5-b9f267c8d3b1.description2: With the political developments of 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. Travelling in the 19th century became easier and more reliable due to the advent of steamships and trains. Westerners travelled to the East not only for touristic purposes, but also for scientific research, history, archaeology or for religious reasons. Western travellers told of their experiences and what they saw in eastern countries in their travel books and they even offer advice about the journey. Istanbul, where East and West meet, has been the subject of many a traveller's book.

02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.name: The Coffee Shop of Cairo
02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.description2: This colourful print depicts a typical 19th century coffeeshop in Cairo. An exclusively male domain, its design was characterised by an open front and wide benches for seating, to allow for easy congregation and the gathering of friends and acquainances. Not only in Cairo, which had over a thousands coffeehouses in Roberts's time, but all over the Middle East, coffeehouses were important social hubs for the exchange of news, entertainment, smoking (customers brought their own pipes and waterpipes) and - not rarely - political dissent. Musicians and storytellers often enhanced the experience further. In this image, the proprietor or an employee of the cafe can be seen serving a beverage in the centre. Interestingly, both the ewer and the large copper cup he uses are of a type usually associated with water, not coffee. Perhaps Roberts introduced these items for artistic effect.

02c575a0-6154-582b-a588-2ae094079d0d.name: *Calligrapher Rıfat Efendi*
02c575a0-6154-582b-a588-2ae094079d0d.description2: Feyhaman Duran was particularly interested in portrait painting and went to Paris in 1910 through the patronage of the Egyptian Prince Abbas Halim Pasha to further his studies in this genre. He greatly profited from the teaching of Paul Richet, professor of anatomy in the School of Fine Arts in Paris. He also attended the Julian Academy where he learned a great deal from Jean-Paul and Albert Laurens. In 1913-14 he worked in the Cormon studio in the School of Fine Arts. Although devoting most of his time to portrait painting, Feyhaman Duran also did paintings of flowers and nudes, but he was definitely most interested in the portrayal of people, and he had very little time for non-figurative painting.

030ea759-beb3-5cac-8d23-28665b5803d8.name: *Meeting between General O'Donnell and Mulay 'Abbas*
030ea759-beb3-5cac-8d23-28665b5803d8.description: Conference between Mulay Abbas, sultan´s brother and General O´Donnell, Spanish President, after battle of Wad-Ras, when Spain claimed the victory and the Moroccan commander Mulay Abbas surrendered. On April 26th, 1860 the representants of Morocco and Spain singed the treaty of peace and the First Spanish Moroccan War ended.

03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.name: Construction Site at Shellal
03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.author: Patrizia Pampana
03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.archival: “Bollettino della Società geografica”, serie IV, 1901, vol. II, n. 6, p. 548
03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.second_name: Egyptian and migrant labourers working on the construction of the first dam on the Nile
03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.description2: In 1900, Count Giulio d’Aspremont, an Italian diplomat, visited the construction site of the first dam across the Nile (today known as the Aswan Low Dam or Old Aswan Dam). He took several pictures of the works and of the monuments on the island of Philae that were going to be submerged by the water. He published some of them on the *Bulletin of the Italian Geographical Society*, where he wrote that up to 2,000 Italian workers were employed in the works (as stone-cutters, miners and masons), out of a total labour force of about 10,000 or 12,000; an Italian village had sprung up on the Nile banks, with modest little houses, trattorias and shops.

03194f3e-048b-5d3e-a6af-514f37ac800f.name: Winged colossus
03194f3e-048b-5d3e-a6af-514f37ac800f.description2: Massive Assyrian winged animals captured the imagination of Victorian England. Large scale reproductions of them were incorporated into “The Assyrian Court” at the Crystal Palace Exhibition.

031df7be-4492-57dc-b989-693ca01a17f1.name: The museum of 'rare possessions'
031df7be-4492-57dc-b989-693ca01a17f1.author: Ibrahim Abdel Aziz
031df7be-4492-57dc-b989-693ca01a17f1.history: Princess Fatma Ismail (1853–1920) was one of Khedive Ismail's daughters. She married Prince Tusun ibn Muhammad Sa`id Pasha, alderman of Egypt, in 1871. She is distinguished from her sisters by her philanthropic contributions to culture and science. Princess Fatma took the initiative of dismissing the university from its financial crisis by providing it with an endowment. She also donated jewellery to provide the university with much-needed cash and land for the campus to be built on. She participated in laying the foundation stone of the university. She passed away before seeing the university built.
031df7be-4492-57dc-b989-693ca01a17f1.keywords: Agricultural museum; Fatma Ismail; Palace; Khedive Ismail; Khedive; agriculture; museum
031df7be-4492-57dc-b989-693ca01a17f1.second_name: Fatma Ismail’s Palace Museum at the Agricultural museum; The Antiquity Collection Museum
031df7be-4492-57dc-b989-693ca01a17f1.description2: This building was once the villa of Fatma Ismail, daughter of Khedive Ismail, and now it is a museum that houses over 500 rare pieces of art dating to the late 19th and early 20th centuries. When the palace was built and then restored, Egyptian architecture was being influenced by the European trends of the time (Italian and French). Italian and French architects were designing and building edifices for the Egyptian elite.

036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.name: An Italian cartoon in support of Ahmad Urabi's movement against foreign control of Egypt's finances
036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.author: Giulia Barrera
036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.description2:
Ahmad Urabi was an Egyptian colonel of peasant origins who led a revolt in 1879-1882 aimed at eliminating foreign control of Egyptian finances and establishing constitutional limits to the Khedive’s authority. John Bull is a recognized national personification of the United Kingdom.  
Caption: “Be careful, merchant! Despite your cannons, your ships and your money, I will be able to teach you that in places where true love for one’s country flourishes, people can make heroic miracles in order to defend their homeland!”  
Part of the Italian public opinion sided with the Egyptians, against the British, since it likened Egyptian struggle with Italian struggle for national unification and self-determination. Ironically, however, in 1882 Italy occupied Massawa, on the Red Sea, and started its own colonial expansion.

036f240e-d388-502f-b085-dcd2a8068418.name: Rashid Pasha Mustafa Mehmet (1802–1858)
036f240e-d388-502f-b085-dcd2a8068418.description2: Portrait of Rashid Pasha. He was born in 1800 in Istanbul and joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs at the age of 20. He served as Ottoman Ambassador in Paris and London. In 1837 he became Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Ottoman Empire. In 1838 he lost his position, but still negotiated as a Turkish diplomat in London, Paris and Berlin. In 1846 he became Grand Vizier and initiated a number of reforms.

03762b34-622e-5cca-85b2-11ca849dd5d2.name: The Hijaz Railway delegations
03762b34-622e-5cca-85b2-11ca849dd5d2.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
03762b34-622e-5cca-85b2-11ca849dd5d2.dates: Late 19th century – beginning of the 20th century
03762b34-622e-5cca-85b2-11ca849dd5d2.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph The Hijaz Railways
03762b34-622e-5cca-85b2-11ca849dd5d2.description2: The Hijaz Railway ran from Damascus to Medina, through the Hijaz region of Saudi Arabia, with a branch line to Haifa on the Mediterranean Sea. It was a part of the Ottoman railway network and was built to extend the line from the Haydarpaşa Terminal in Istanbul beyond Damascus to the holy city of Mecca. The main purpose of the railway was to establish a connection between the capital of the Ottoman Empire and the seat of the Islamic Caliphate, and Hijaz in Arabia, the site of the holiest shrines of Islam and the holy city of Mecca, the destination of the Hajj annual pilgrimage. Another important reason was to improve the economic and political integration of the distant Arabian provinces into the Ottoman state, and to facilitate the transportation of military forces.

03769685-706c-53a4-99dd-0ddabeddce9c.name: *The Attack of Smârdan*
03769685-706c-53a4-99dd-0ddabeddce9c.description2: Romania, that in the second half of the 19th century was still under Ottoman sovereignty, participated in the Russian-Ottoman of 1877-1878 war on Russia’s side. In May 1877 the Parliament declared Romania’s independence, which was recognized by the Ottoman Empire and the Great Powers at the peace congress organized in Berlin after the conflict (June – July 1878). When Romania entered the war, Nicolae Grigorescu was one of the painters hired to accompany the Romanian army. One of his best known works depicts the victory that the Romanian soldiers won against the Ottomans at Smârdan (24 January 1878). The painting, which has several variants, was based on others’ accounts because Grigorescu was sick and could not be present on the front when the battle took place.

0377755d-a4a5-57ef-8cca-716b1fdb2ad1.name: Document recording the purchase of steamships
0377755d-a4a5-57ef-8cca-716b1fdb2ad1.description: A record from the archive of correspondence between the Sultan of Morocco Mulay al-Hasan I and his Minister of Foreign Affairs and representative in Tangier, Muhammad ibn al-‘Arabi al-Torres. It details Morocco’s order, from Italy, for the construction of a warship, the payment terms, constraints and currency exchange rates. In 1891, Morocco purchased four warships and a number of steamships.
0377755d-a4a5-57ef-8cca-716b1fdb2ad1.keywords: Italians in Morocco; industrialists; Italian industrialists; war; warfare; changes in warfare; arms; warship; steamship; trade; economy; Italian-Moroccan relations; diplomacy; technical innovations

03fa93d0-4ba6-5345-9362-3c66f5efb5d1.name: Necklace
03fa93d0-4ba6-5345-9362-3c66f5efb5d1.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
03fa93d0-4ba6-5345-9362-3c66f5efb5d1.keywords: zebra fish; concave; Ottoman; coins; silver
03fa93d0-4ba6-5345-9362-3c66f5efb5d1.description2: A zebra fish chain with a concave silver Turkish coins and two metal circles at the end to fix the necklace on the hat and dangle down the neck. Silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. Jordan's economy relied on trade and crafts; new waves of people started to come to Jordan and began to settle for these purposes. This object reflects the diverse population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It also demonstrates personal attire, fashion, local costumes and rites.

04456e8e-b665-5aa7-96a4-825dc6689071.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph map
04456e8e-b665-5aa7-96a4-825dc6689071.description2: One of the world's largest photo archives, Abdülhamid II's photo archives – knows as the Yildiz Albums – contain about 37 thousand pictures from that period of the Ottoman Empire. Abdülhamid II was the 34th Sultan of the Ottoman Empire and the last Sultan to exert effective autocratic control over the fracturing state. He oversaw a period of decline in the power and extent of the empire, including widespread pogroms and government massacres against the minorities of the empire (named the Hamidian massacres, after him) as well as an assassination attempt. He ruled from 31 August 1876 until he was deposed shortly after the 1908 Young Turk Revolution, on 27 April 1909.

04c6becd-fdd7-5c20-9596-b48f8a6ce25a.name: Traditional bridal costume and jewellery
04c6becd-fdd7-5c20-9596-b48f8a6ce25a.author: Gordanche Vidinic, ethnologist
04c6becd-fdd7-5c20-9596-b48f8a6ce25a.keywords: Costume; accessories; headdress; fez; wedding; marriage
04c6becd-fdd7-5c20-9596-b48f8a6ce25a.description2: This set of traditional clothing gives an overall picture of the universally recognized aesthetics displayed in the festive women’s outfits in Macedonia in the 19th century. Bridal costumes worn in the area of Dolni Polog were distinctive for the great number of varied garments they comprised. The costume, consisting of a *fusta*, a kind of undershirt; a *bunda*, a thicker undergarment; chemise; tunic; vest and other garments, was abundantly decorated with embroidery. It was also richly embellished with jewellery and accessorized with distinctive headdress. Even the headdress included more than one article: a fez made of red baize, a hair band called a *votus* adorned with strings of coins as well as a transparent silk scarf decorated with embroidery, fringes and sequins.

04e56c00-ff8a-5334-9dea-eb0e9fc10644.name: *Kjustek* for men's watch
04e56c00-ff8a-5334-9dea-eb0e9fc10644.author: Milena Petrovic, ethnologist
04e56c00-ff8a-5334-9dea-eb0e9fc10644.keywords: Men's jewellery; kjustek; metalwork; accessories; silver; filigree
04e56c00-ff8a-5334-9dea-eb0e9fc10644.second_name: Men's ornament worn on the chests
04e56c00-ff8a-5334-9dea-eb0e9fc10644.description2: Unlike the diversity of women’s jewellery, there was smaller number of articles of adornment used by men. Male jewellery was, however, rather massive, more precious and more costly in its production. Besides rings, especially impressive were massive silver *kjusteks* (watch chains), which were worn suspended on the chests. This *kjustek* is a nice piece of the jewellery worn by men, showing clearly some elements of Oriental influence. *Kjusteks* and other pieces of metal jewellery used to be worn by men in towns, whereas the jewellery of men in villages was mostly made of tiny beads (*monistra*).

051009e2-86ca-5d85-b8dc-8901f452c3c4.keywords: Pilgrimage; pilgrims; Christian pilgrimage; Jewish pilgrimage; Palestine; Holy Land; Jerusalem; sacred places; travel; travel book; Ottoman Palestine
051009e2-86ca-5d85-b8dc-8901f452c3c4.description2: This colour illustration is included in the book *Palestine Past and Present* by Laura Jewry Valentine. In addition to the illustration (which is similar to other 19th-century illustrations of this site), the book provides a description of a prayer the Jews performed at the Western Wall every Friday at three o' clock, and the great importance ascribed to the wall as a symbol of lost unity.

055fd98c-bc6c-5a97-9aae-e3c3ab6ea7fb.name: Plan of Bullring of Campo Pequeno, Lisbon
055fd98c-bc6c-5a97-9aae-e3c3ab6ea7fb.keywords: Rediscovering the Past; Cities; Urban Spaces
055fd98c-bc6c-5a97-9aae-e3c3ab6ea7fb.description2: Built in an area assigned to the Casa Pia by the city of Lisbon in 1889 Praça de Touros do Campo Pequeno (Campo Pequeno Bullring) was designed by the architect António José Dias da Silva (1848-1912) and inspired by the Madrid's bullring. Praça de Touros do Campo Pequeno opened its doors on August 18, 1892, with a gala show.

057b0a91-5753-5a0f-a506-60b096d9eeb0.name: Saliha Sultan Fountain
057b0a91-5753-5a0f-a506-60b096d9eeb0.author: Bahattin Öztuncay
057b0a91-5753-5a0f-a506-60b096d9eeb0.description2: Robertson’s photographs of landscapes and monuments were usually printed in a roughly 25 by 30cm format. In the early years of his career as a photographer, he appears to have preferred the albumen-on-glass method of taking negatives, switching to the wet collodion process around 1855. For his positive prints, he used salt paper until about 1858; after that, prints were made on albumen paper even if they were made from negatives taken before that year. Robertson’s photographs are concentrated mainly in and around the districts known as Sultanahmet, Beyoğlu, Galata and Tophane today. This photo captures the Saliha Sultan Fountain in Galata.

057cb072-73f1-5597-b0c3-f4145e5d0880.name: *British Soldiers Near Selimiye Barracks in Scutari Waiting to be Dispatched to Crimea*
057cb072-73f1-5597-b0c3-f4145e5d0880.author: Bahattin Öztuncay
057cb072-73f1-5597-b0c3-f4145e5d0880.keywords: Crimean War; war photojounalism; British forces in Crimean War
057cb072-73f1-5597-b0c3-f4145e5d0880.description2: Robertson's photographs of the Crimean War represent an important chapter in his career. The Crimean War was the first war in history to be extensively covered by press correspondents. The photographs taken by James Robertson and Roger Fenton put them in the ranks of the world’s first war photojournalists. James Robertson’s first photographs related to the Crimean War were actually taken in Istanbul. After England’s declaration of war on 27 March 1854, British and colonial forces dispatched to the front by sea began gathering at Selimiye in Üsküdar and neighbouring districts in April and May.

05b44d2d-3b76-5151-b3a6-9f62194bb1f1.name: *An Anxious Hour*
05b44d2d-3b76-5151-b3a6-9f62194bb1f1.dimensions: Height: 11.875 in estimate, Width: 16 in estimate, Height: 51 cm framed, Width: 62 cm framed
05b44d2d-3b76-5151-b3a6-9f62194bb1f1.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
05b44d2d-3b76-5151-b3a6-9f62194bb1f1.keywords: Children; illness; childhood; health; painting; women
05b44d2d-3b76-5151-b3a6-9f62194bb1f1.description2: Farmer specialised in genre scenes, often with sentimental subjects. *An Anxious Hour* reflects the high death rate of Victorian children from disease. The sitter is probably the artist's sister Emily, a watercolourist who painted similar subjects.

05d601e6-b672-5f09-a5af-f912a7e4475e.name: The Silk Factory
05d601e6-b672-5f09-a5af-f912a7e4475e.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
05d601e6-b672-5f09-a5af-f912a7e4475e.history: The silk industry was a very important part of the Lebanese economy - the transportation of silk and silk cocoons from Beirut to Marseille, for example, laid the foundations for maritime trade agencies in Lebanon. The loans and grants made to intermediaries and traders wishing to buy silk cocoons from farmers were some of the first financial traders, which later led to the establishment of the first Lebanese bank and to the development of the Port of Beirut. In Gaston Ducousso's book, *The Silk Industry in Syria and Lebanon*, published in 1912, the French Consul in Beirut counted no less than 183 spinning mills in Lebanon. In 1841, a team of spinners was brought from France to train young women in the art of spinning silk, something which was particularly foreign to the rural areas, where young women were not traditionally employed in this form of labour.
05d601e6-b672-5f09-a5af-f912a7e4475e.architects: Prosper, Nicolas, Joseph and Antoine Fortuné Portalis
05d601e6-b672-5f09-a5af-f912a7e4475e.description2: In 1841, Prosper, Nicolas, Joseph and Antoine Fortuné Portalis built the first spinning mill for reeling cocoons, in Btater in the Chouf region.

05d7791f-fc59-5e62-bfee-252400caeca3.name: Portrait of Shaykh 'Abd al-Basit al-Fakhuri
05d7791f-fc59-5e62-bfee-252400caeca3.description: Born in Beirut in 1824, Shaykh 'Abd al-Basit al-Fakhuri studied under great masters such as Shaykh Muhammad al-Hur in the Great Umari Mosque in Beirut. He quickly gained a brilliant reputation and begun teaching before the age of 25. He remained a mufti until his death in 1905. Many of his manuscripts, and a book on *hadith* were found, unpublished, after his death.
05d7791f-fc59-5e62-bfee-252400caeca3.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader

0659eb21-0d9f-5b11-ae51-0ba0f6eea1f1.name: Reverent Baboon with Pharaoh figure
0659eb21-0d9f-5b11-ae51-0ba0f6eea1f1.description: The loud rejoicing of the Hamadryas baboon at the sunrise in its rocky habitat served as a model for the Egyptian celebration of the ascent and descent of the sun at the critical stages of its cycle. Baboons with upraised hands – the Egyptian gesture of reverence – became symbols for the “eastern souls”, the gods who cheer the sun at its appearance above the horizon. The king joins these gods in his role as sun priest.
0659eb21-0d9f-5b11-ae51-0ba0f6eea1f1.dates: 18th Dyn. Amenophis II, 1454-1419 BC; acquired in 1865/66

06623ef3-6331-5463-b5c0-79f3249d4f5d.name: Painting of Ahmed Pacha Bey
06623ef3-6331-5463-b5c0-79f3249d4f5d.holder: Musée d’Histoire Moderne et Contemporaine de Kassar Saïd
06623ef3-6331-5463-b5c0-79f3249d4f5d.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
06623ef3-6331-5463-b5c0-79f3249d4f5d.keywords: Oil on canvas; Ahmed Pacha Bey; Charles Gleyre
06623ef3-6331-5463-b5c0-79f3249d4f5d.materials: Canvas, wood, coloured pigments, gold leaf
06623ef3-6331-5463-b5c0-79f3249d4f5d.description2: This oil on canvas portrait by the Swiss artist Charles Gleyre (1806–1874) depicts Ahmed Pacha Bey, the ruling prince of Tunisia at the time (1837–1855). He is dressed in official uniform, with red trousers with a gold strip and a black overcoat with gold epaulets, and is wearing the *muchir*'s insignia round his neck, and the Ordre du Sang, the Nichan al-Dam, and the Grand Croix de la Légion d'Honneur medals on the left of his chest. His torso his divided in two by a shimmering red sash of honour, his black and gold sword hangs off his belt on the left-hand side, and he is wearing a red chechia on his head. This painting is evidence of an active diplomatic relationship between the Palais du Bardo and the European chancelleries.

069c2465-1b42-5572-8535-19f44b1fc837.name: Archaeological excavations
069c2465-1b42-5572-8535-19f44b1fc837.description2:
This photograph shows the entrance to a tomb in the region of al-Kouban in Nubia, one of the archaeological sites excavated by James E. Quibell in 1882. The tomb has a vaulted ceiling made of mud brick, and the entrance marks the expansion of the tomb building from the inside.  
The photo is from a gelatine print negative, and it was included in the archive of the archaeological area of Saqqara, Giza.

06aabaa5-8fbd-543d-ac79-07b3315474de.name: The Statue of The God Bes
06aabaa5-8fbd-543d-ac79-07b3315474de.keywords: Istanbul Archaeological Museum; Tiled Kiosk; The God Bes
06aabaa5-8fbd-543d-ac79-07b3315474de.description2: A large statue of dwarf God Bes is located in the Aessos Works Hall. Bes was an ancient Egyptian dwarf god. He was a complex being who was both a deity and a demonic fighter. He was a god of war, yet he was also a patron of childbirth and the home, and was associated with sexuality, humour, music and dancing. Bes also became popular with the Phoenicians and in Cyprus.

06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.name: Alexandria: The Consuls’ Square Rebuilt
06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.author: Patrizia Pampana, Giulia Barrera
06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.archival: Licurgo Santoni, *Alto Egitto e Nubia*, Roma, Modes e Mendei, 1905.
06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.second_name: The Consuls' Square in Alexandria (Egypt) rebuilt after being destroyed by a fire in 1882
06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.description2: The large, rectangular square initially know under the French name “Place des Consuls” (later as Muhammad 'Ali Square), was officially inaugurated in 1860. It was designed by Francesco Mancini, chief engineer of the “Commissione d’ornato” (Board of Works), a committee set up in 1834 by Muhammad 'Ali (ruler of Egypt in 1805-1848), and modelled after similar urban-planning committees already functioning in some Italian cities. In 1872, an equestrian statue of Muhammad 'Ali was erected in the square, which took his name. In July 1882, after anti-foreign rioting in Alexandria, the British fleet heavily bombed the city, causing major destructions to the buildings surrounding the square.

en: Ghoneim, Mohamed, “Alexandrian Culture in Modern Times: Egyptian Identity and Cosmopolitan Aspects”, in Kenneth Hamma (ed.), *Alexandria and Alexandrianism*, Malibu, CA: J. Paul Getty Museum, 1996: 285–301.

Re, Lucia, “Alexandria Revisited: Colonialism and the Egyptian Works of Enrico Pea and Giuseppe Ungaretti”, in Patrizia Palumbo (ed.), *A Place in the Sun: Africa in Italian Colonial Culture from Post-unification to the Present*, Berkeley, CA: University of California Press, 2003: 163–96.

07024cd6-c5bb-5d57-96ec-903ad7f248c4.keywords: Paleoethnology; archaeology; exploration; anthropology; natural history; material culture; academy; Jesuits; Egypt; Egyptology; collection; collector; exoticism; curiosities; wunderkammer; Museum Kircherianum; Baroque; languages; Arabic

07024cd6-c5bb-5d57-96ec-903ad7f248c4.description2:
The origins, in terms of scientific activity and conservation, of the Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico "Luigi Pigorini" in Rome, can be traced back to the foundation in 1875 of the “Regio Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico di Roma" (Royal National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography). Initially the museum was located in a wing of the Palazzo del Collegio Romano built in the late 16th century by the Society of Jesus.  
This rare image represents the old arrangement of one of the rooms of the Roman College, where the collection of antiquities and curiosities gathered together by Father Athanasius Kircher was kept after the foundation of the museum. According to the intentions of its founder, Luigi Pigorini, the purpose of this new institution was not only to gather together the remains of Italian prehistoric culture and the "primitive" cultures of other European and non-European peoples in a "central" museum located in the new capital of the Kingdom, but above all to support, promote and participate in research by paleontologists in Italy.

0703f771-513c-549f-8e72-02d81616e8d9.description2: This pearl merchant's chest, known in the region as bishtakha, was an indispensable item of a pearl merchant's profession, as it contained not only all his equipment, but also his valuable bags of pearls. Made of hardwood and often elaborately decorated, these chests could come in different sizes and were designed to hold pearling scales with their agate weights, scoops, graded sieves, small discrete boxes for cash - often hidden in secret compartments - bags of pearls and the so-called chao book, used to calculate - by means of detailed tables - the value of specific pearls on the basis of their weight.

077c68fe-2e6b-58e1-8e7b-c457e2fe3a33.description2: Unlike the metal jewellery worn in towns, which was produced by goldsmiths, jewellery and other articles of adornment from rural areas were made by women themselves, mostly of canvas, *monistra* (tiny beads in varied colours) and by use of the fruits of the nature, flowers, etc.

0789647b-9e7e-5620-892e-044eb391df8f.name: Unicellular House: 'Kukh'
0789647b-9e7e-5620-892e-044eb391df8f.description: This kind of habitation provides only the most basic functions of a house: shelter and warmth. It has no outdoor spaces, and the windows and doors are generally very small. Even today, domestic or social activities (such as cooking, washing, eating, relaxing, working or receiving guests) in these houses generally take place outdoors, either outside the front door or to the side of the house under a canopy or in the shade of a tree. The interior was not divided in any particular way, and divisions between rooms were traditionally created my movable objects, such as cabinets, curtains or wooden partitions. In the *kukh*s of today, solid walls have taken their place.
0789647b-9e7e-5620-892e-044eb391df8f.author: Jeff El-Msanne, David Andos
0789647b-9e7e-5620-892e-044eb391df8f.history: The *kukh* is a modest house. It was the basic model for a traditional house in the agricultural suburbs of Beirut. *Kukh*s were popular until the mid-19th century and were generally inhabited by farmers and their families. They also functioned as temporary shelter for livestock or domestic animals.

078cfe51-b4db-5203-b6c8-54fede56f98d.name: *Bayt Niyadu, Damascus*
078cfe51-b4db-5203-b6c8-54fede56f98d.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
078cfe51-b4db-5203-b6c8-54fede56f98d.second_name: Inhabitants in the courtyard demonstrating the new style of decoration and clothing
078cfe51-b4db-5203-b6c8-54fede56f98d.description2: Like the Lisbuna House, Bayt Niyadu saw two major construction phases, namely, in the 18th and late 19th century. It was refurbished as so many houses between 1865 and 1872 and features marble ornamentation similar to the one in Bayt Lisbuna´s courtyard. These houses are from the layout typical "traditional" courtyard houses of the region. However, the Niyadu House became known (also on postcards) for its richness and abundance of up to date Ottoman decor. The owners expressed their Damascene modernity proudly to the outside – also in this picture: the gentlemen sports a European-style dinner jacket and the lady a mid-length skirt, teamed with a withe blouse in the latest fashion. This transformation of private forms of urban live – notice also the brand new and modern electrical lightening in the "traditional" courtyard – can be seen throughout the city and is an important example of a local expression of global modernity.

07fa4973-f69d-57f4-8e6d-caeb88f75252.materials: Cotton fabric, *srma* – silver and gold-wrapped thread, braids. Buckles: silver, hammering, decorative stones
07fa4973-f69d-57f4-8e6d-caeb88f75252.second_name: Articles of adornment worn at the waist – *pafti*
07fa4973-f69d-57f4-8e6d-caeb88f75252.description2: Buckles were the most prominent articles of adornment worn by Macedonian women. They were also the most frequently worn pieces of jewellery, having been an inevitable element of folk costumes in all parts of Macedonia. Combining functionality and aesthetics, buckles were also considered to play a protective role. The diverse shapes – round, rectangular, leaf-shaped, etc., as well as the exquisite style of their decorating, show the remarkable skill and talent of goldsmiths producing them. These buckles consist of two slightly concave round plates joined with a little round piece used for fastening. They are adorned with decorative stones and decorated with geometric patterns applied by hammering. The belt is made of cotton fabric decorated with geometric and floral patterns by application of silver and gold-wrapped thread and braids.

0801264d-8475-5c87-a800-17b6d0cc190e.name: The drawings of Janissary clothes from The Album of Mecmua-i Tesavir-i Osmaniye (The collection of Ottoman Pictures)
0801264d-8475-5c87-a800-17b6d0cc190e.holder: Military Museum and Cultural Centre Command
0801264d-8475-5c87-a800-17b6d0cc190e.description2: Arif Mehmed Pasha is considered one of the leaders of the western style of painting in Turkey. He developed a talent for drawing and produced a series of pictures detailing the clothes Ottoman state officials wore. He prepared these pictures under the name *Mecmua-i Tesavir-i Osmaniyye*. Although his work was supposed to come out in 12 volumes, only one volume was actually published in French in Paris in 1863 and in Turkish the same year. The other 11 volumes have been lost. The published volume is considered to be the first illustrated book in Turkey. What is amazing is the praise heaped onto Arif Mehmed Pasha for his portraits, the harmony of their colours and tones, the maturity of attitude and delicate detail, the artist’s control over his pen and watercolours. The clothing reflects the time when the Janissaries were still on the scene (before 1826 when the corps was disbanded).

088cf3bb-ffc3-56ca-8a23-9d69924c19fa.description2: The Port of Alexandria during the departure of King Fu`ad on a trip to Europe. The Eastern Port of Alexandria is one of the oldest ports in the world. It was established in 2000 BCE, at the ancient village of Rakotis, to serve the coastal areas of the Pharos island (now the area of Ra's al-Tin in Alexandria). To its west lies the Bay of Anfushi.

Built in 1859, it connected Tétouan to the River Martil or Rio Martin as the Spanish – who built the railway – named it. In 1887, the Belgian government ordered a small locomotive factory, based in Munich, to build some rolling stock: Krauss 74, No. 1769.

08c133b3-6259-5695-84a5-63de2f4fdb57.description2: A number of important political and literary figures moved abroad during Napoléon III's authoritarian rule. This was the case with Victor Hugo, who left France between 1852 and 1870 as he refused to live under the reign of, "Napoléon le Petit", as he liked to call him.

08d3aed6-3599-5046-816b-66df7858d6a8.name: *The Sultan’s Horses* (Drawing 19 for the *XX Dessins* album)
08d3aed6-3599-5046-816b-66df7858d6a8.description: This drawing by Amadeo de Souza-Cardoso forms part of an album, *XX Dessins*, which was published in 1912 and represents a key point of breakthrough for the artist. The context of the work can be explained by his interest in the Western primitivists, the influence of African art, the experiences that he exchanged with Brancusi and Modigliani, and his study of Henri Rousseau’s work. The artist aims to present a demarcated image of his own identity: in an elegantly sophisticated picture replete with medieval imagery, he produces an original work that explores volumes, dynamic forms, and the sense of speed. It was this clearly defined image that Amadeo presented at the Armory Show in 1913, where his work achieved great success in both critical and market terms.

091c2bb3-6009-5f5c-bff2-8e5c54938f6c.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority
091c2bb3-6009-5f5c-bff2-8e5c54938f6c.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
091c2bb3-6009-5f5c-bff2-8e5c54938f6c.description2: The slightly confusing title of this print by David Roberts actually refers to the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem, first commissioned in 327 AD by the Emperor Constantine and his mother Helena. at the spot where it is believed Jesus was born. The view captures the area before the iconostasis shielding the main altar in the eastern apse of the church, as well as - below on the right - the south-eastern entrance to the Grotto of the Nativity.The Church of the Nativity is one of the foremost pilgrimage sites for Christians and would have been a highlight on the itinerary of European travellers to the Holy Land. As is typical for his works, Roberts exaggerates the proportions of the architecture in relation to the human figures, which appear dwarfed by the majesty and monumentality of the structures that surround them.

0938866e-9a77-5d93-86b4-888bd58845d1.name: *Constantinople*
0938866e-9a77-5d93-86b4-888bd58845d1.description2: With the political developments of 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. Travelling in the 19th century became easier and more reliable due to the advent of steamships and trains. Westerners travelled to the East not only for touristic purposes, but also for scientific research, history, archaeology or for religious reasons. Western travellers told of their experiences and what they saw in eastern countries in their travel books and they even offer advice about the journey. Istanbul, where East and West meet, has been the subject of many a traveller's book.

Although it reproduces a traditional technique, this tile panel exemplifies the need for modernization of stores and public buildings which took place in main cities throughout Portugal by the beginning of the 20th century.

0a0e3c68-6be2-5140-b568-bf800fe28f33.holder: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation /Sharjah Museums Authority

0a0e3c68-6be2-5140-b568-bf800fe28f33.description2: This print was originally published in 'La Ilustracion Espanola y Americana', a newspaper published in Madrid on the 15th of April, 1882. Entitled 'La Peregrinacion religiosa de los mahometanos: Vista general de la Meca, del patio y claustro de la mesquita El-Haram y de la Santa Kaaba', it was copied from the first known photograph (at the time) depicting the Makkah precinct, taken - according to the newspaper - by the English traveller Mr [John Fryer Thomas] Keane.  Keane (1854-1937) was a clergyman, who converted to Islam and visited Makkah in 1877. In 1881, he published two books about his experiences in the Hijaz, 'Six Months in Meccah' and 'My Journey to Medinah'. The image shows the courtyard of the Makkah mosque with hundreds of pilgrims clustering around the Ka'bah at the centre. Beyond, the hills of Makkah with their traditional houses, many of them multistoreyed, can be seen.

0a226934-adb7-5611-ac1e-769b4276935b.name: *Mount Tabor*
0a226934-adb7-5611-ac1e-769b4276935b.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
0a226934-adb7-5611-ac1e-769b4276935b.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
0a226934-adb7-5611-ac1e-769b4276935b.description2: This depiction of Mount Tabor by the American artist John Douglas Woodward carries the caption 'Mount Tabor. Bearing among the Arabs, like so many other mountains, only the general name 'Jebel et Tur'. The scene suggests a rugged, primeval landscape untouched by modern humanity, the mystically lit, driven clouds that half veil the mounting evoking a spiritual and at the same time awe-inspiring atmosphere well suited to an important biblical site. In popular Christian tradition: Mount Tabor was associated with the Transfiguration of Christ. At the same time the mountain was to prove of historical importance, too.  In 1799, during the time of Napoleon Bonaparte's expedition in the area, the valley between Mount Tabor and the Moreh Hill saw a decisive battle in which a French force of about 3,000 soldiers under the command of Napoleon and General Jean Baptiste Kléber faced a Mamluk force of about 20,000 soldiers.

0a232d6e-3ce2-5412-be8a-b9cb0af2bff7.name: Tile
0a232d6e-3ce2-5412-be8a-b9cb0af2bff7.description2: Kütahya was the second most important ceramic production centre after İznik due to the rich clay deposits in the area. Although there was a decline in ceramic production at the beginning of the 19th century, in the last quarter of that same century production was revived and new designs inspired by İznik ceramics were produced.

0a469d79-a94f-5097-a3cc-17e2bdc452a1.name: Balkan immigrants village at Sivrihisar
0a469d79-a94f-5097-a3cc-17e2bdc452a1.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
0a469d79-a94f-5097-a3cc-17e2bdc452a1.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; History of Ottoman Empire; Balkan wars; migrations
0a469d79-a94f-5097-a3cc-17e2bdc452a1.description2: The civilian population living in the Balkans was forced to migrate to Anatolia due to the Balkan Wars at the end of the 18th century: the 1821 Mora rebellion, the 1856 Crimean war, the 1864 Russian-Caucasian war, the 1877-1878 Ottoman-Russian War, the 1896-97 Crete Rebellion, the 1912-13 Balkan Wars, World War I from 1914 to 1918 and the 1919-22 Greek-Turkish War. These wars resulted in mass migrations. The Ottoman Empire lost almost all its European territories west of the River Maritsa, drawing present day Turkey's western border. A large influx of Turks started to flee into the Ottoman heartland as a result of the lost lands. By 1914, the remaining core region of the Ottoman Empire had experienced a population increase of around 2.5 million because of the flood of immigration from the Balkans.

0a489e52-7566-5a35-a21d-e7338d8cc6b4.name: Jar with enamel decoration
0a489e52-7566-5a35-a21d-e7338d8cc6b4.holder: Museo Artistico Industriale, National Gallery of Ancient Art in Palazzo Barberini
0a489e52-7566-5a35-a21d-e7338d8cc6b4.author: Marina Minozzi
0a489e52-7566-5a35-a21d-e7338d8cc6b4.keywords: Applied arts; manufacture; craftsmanship; museums of applied arts; model; reproduction; motifs; collection; collector; glasswork; Murano; Islamic art; production of applied arts in Europe in the Islamic mode; minor arts; enamelling
0a489e52-7566-5a35-a21d-e7338d8cc6b4.description2: The Museum of Industrial Arts (M.A.I.) was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century and as a training school for specializing artisans. The idea was part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history passed down from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic traditions in the Middle Ages. In the 19th century there was also a rebirth of the Murano glass for different reasons. The jar with enamelled decorations, white flowers and green leaves was made in Murano and dates from the beginning of the 20th century. It shows evolution of forms and techniques through the new ideas coming from Art Nouveau and the diffusion of polychrome enamels.
0a489e52-7566-5a35-a21d-e7338d8cc6b4.holding_institution_org: Museo Artistico Industriale presso la Galleria nazionale d’arte antica in Palazzo Barberini

0a4f03ff-bf1b-52e6-aede-b7826456b1d7.name: Rossio Railway Station
0a4f03ff-bf1b-52e6-aede-b7826456b1d7.history: Rossio railway station, commissioned by Conselho Superior de Obras Púbicas was designed in 1886-87 by Portuguese architect José Luís Monteiro. It was built in Rossio, a central and busy square of Lisbon Downtown. A tunnel was excavated under the city and is considered one of the most important works of engineering in Portugal dating from the 19th century; it was completed in 1890.
0a4f03ff-bf1b-52e6-aede-b7826456b1d7.keywords: Lisbon; Architecture; Romantic Style; Iberian Arab memory; railway station
0a4f03ff-bf1b-52e6-aede-b7826456b1d7.description2: Rossio railway station (Lisbon) was designed by the Portuguese architect José Luís Monteiro. The construction begun in 1886 and was inaugurated on 23 November of 1890. Located in the historical center of Lisbon, the Rossio Station follows the Neo-Manueline architectural style, and is an important Lisbon building of the late Romantic style  from the 19th century.

0b0283d8-2b68-513e-ac6c-83c7af076357.name: *Street scribe*
0b0283d8-2b68-513e-ac6c-83c7af076357.description:
This illustration is included in a book written by James Augustus Saint John, a British writer and traveller who visited Egypt and Nubia in 1832 and published a book about the places and people he had seen. The author focused on details aiming at illustrating (according to his point of view) the life of the country.  
  
This illustration of a street scribe shows how traditional jobs were still active in Egyptian society at a time when the country was undergoing political, social and administrative changes under Muhammad ‘Ali Pasha. The illustration suggests an unintentional comparison with European countries at that time, where although social, political and technical changes were also happening, urban and rural society continued to retain traditional jobs like the street scribe.
0b0283d8-2b68-513e-ac6c-83c7af076357.author: Maria Francesca Carvelli (MWNF)
0b0283d8-2b68-513e-ac6c-83c7af076357.archival: Saint John, James Augustus, *Egypt and Nubia, with illustrations*, London, 1845, p. 234
0b0283d8-2b68-513e-ac6c-83c7af076357.keywords: Work; traditional jobs; workers' condition; alphabetisation; Egyptian society; European society; travel; book; Egypt; Nubia; Sudan; innovations

0b5e2b9b-6dd4-501c-9d61-0af91a0c8de8.name: 5 May 1919, bank employees on strike [at the trade unions building,  Rue de la Grange-aux-Belles, 10e arrondissement, Paris.
0b5e2b9b-6dd4-501c-9d61-0af91a0c8de8.description2: The difficulties in returning to peacetime society after the end of the First World War created huge shifts in the social fabric of Paris. The city saw continuous strikes from May to July 1919. The most numerically significant was the steelworkers' strike, but all sectors were affected, as we can see from this photo, in which bank workers protest the "high cost of living" and "insufficient salaries".

0b61c9ae-ef04-5d1e-af0b-b7e4ab248173.name: Type-writing machine
0b61c9ae-ef04-5d1e-af0b-b7e4ab248173.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Dragan Georgiev, historian (consultant)
0b61c9ae-ef04-5d1e-af0b-b7e4ab248173.description2: Dimitrija Chupovski (1878-1940) was born in Papradishte near Veles, R. Macedonia in 1878. He lived in Krushevo and acquired his education in Belgrade and St. Petersburg. He was a renowned Macedonian lexicographer, textbook writer and philologist who prepared the modern grammar of Macedonian language. Chupovski also worked out the first Macedonian-Russian dictionary.

0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.name: Misrata [Libya]. In the Home of Gabrielli, Agent of the Society of Maritime Services [Società dei servizi marittimi]
0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.author: Patrizia Pampana, Giulia Barrera
0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.third_name: *Misràta. In casa di Gabrielli, agente della Società dei servizi marittimi*
0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.description2:
In 19th and early 20th century Africa, the nature of the relations between European men and African women varied dramatically according to the different power relations between the partners. In colonial situations, the legal subordination of the colonised people put African women in particularly weak positions vis-à-vis European men, generally resulting in very exploitative relationships. In countries that were not under European rule, more balanced relationships could develop.  
This picture shows a mixed family in Libya before the onset of Italian colonialism. The setting of the picture suggests that the Libyan woman enjoyed respect and status within the family: the woman and her children are sitting on chairs, surrounded by persons who appear to be domestic servants, and the Italian man is standing behind her, looking at their children.

0b7f2149-f01d-5891-815e-947600259db6.name: *The drilling of an artesian well*
0b7f2149-f01d-5891-815e-947600259db6.artist: Artist: G. Dascher; engraver: L. Geisler
0b7f2149-f01d-5891-815e-947600259db6.description2: The purpose of the album *Les Colonies Françaises* was to highlight, amongst other things, the French "achievements" and technological innovations in the colonies, and thus legitimise their rule. This image shows the construction of an artesian well in Tunisia in the 19th century. In reality, however, this type of well was built by the French army in order to appease the populations in agricultural areas and thus better control them.

0b914ea4-3750-5949-ba83-6be97904425d.name: The fundamental pact
0b914ea4-3750-5949-ba83-6be97904425d.author: Bechir Yazidi
0b914ea4-3750-5949-ba83-6be97904425d.description2: This foundational text was drawn up by Mohamed Bey of the Husainid dynasty (1855–1859) under the pressure of the French and English consuls. They had the aim of either adopting or adapting the reforms introduced in Istanbul which required them to provide non-Muslim subjects with semi-secular services, such as the establishment of mixed tribunals avoiding the strict application of the Quran, and also ensured free trade for France and England.

0ba121fb-d876-5f66-b258-176f999c7959.name: *Seated Moor*
0ba121fb-d876-5f66-b258-176f999c7959.description: This small oil painting was painted in Valencia in a very early date (1880–1884) and is an example of Sorolla’s early works, when he still painted small pieces that follow the taste of the time. This Orientalist topic was very popular in Europe at the end of the century and the paintings sold very well. The inspiration was not from travel or cultural knowledge, but instead was the result of studying engravings, watercolours, and other paintings of the time. The production of this type of topic in Sorolla is very short and almost all of it dates to his early years.
0ba121fb-d876-5f66-b258-176f999c7959.author: Covadonga Pitarch
0ba121fb-d876-5f66-b258-176f999c7959.keywords: Orientalist painting; Spain; Formation of painters

0ba224c3-c5fc-59df-943c-70ba396625a7.name: Lambaesis. Inside the praetorium
0ba224c3-c5fc-59df-943c-70ba396625a7.description2: This photograph belonged to Georges Sirot (1898–1977), one of the first great collectors of photographs. Lambaesis was a military town in Roman Africa, rediscovered by archaeologists.

0ba2e663-9318-562e-9c2a-099d167e8112.name: Earrings
0ba2e663-9318-562e-9c2a-099d167e8112.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
0ba2e663-9318-562e-9c2a-099d167e8112.author: Huda Kilani
0ba2e663-9318-562e-9c2a-099d167e8112.keywords: 23 karat gold; rosettes; coral; Ottoman coins
0ba2e663-9318-562e-9c2a-099d167e8112.description2: 23-karat gold earrings from South Palestine (Beer Sheba), with red stones, blue talismans mounted on rosettes of coral, and gold Ottoman coins (dated 1808). Silver jewellery was the most common because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. Silver or gold jewellery was part of the dowry given by the groom to the bride. The material (gold or silver) and even the coins used as pieces of jewellery were an indirect statement of the financial status of the groom.

0bdb3920-5c44-5859-a7de-be6f63a099b9.name: *Raft Conveying Winged Bull to Baghdad*
0bdb3920-5c44-5859-a7de-be6f63a099b9.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
0bdb3920-5c44-5859-a7de-be6f63a099b9.description2: Layard describes the removal of the winged bulls from the site of the mound of Nimrud in Nineveh and its remains, 1849, from where they had lain for approximately the last 2,730 years. They were carefully loaded on to rafts, made in the traditional way of using hundreds of inflated goat and sheep-skins supporting a wooden superstructure. Layard (who had learnt Arabic and Persian) recruited the crew locally, as he had done with his workforce. In April 1847, he sent them floating with the current, off on a six hundred mile journey down the river Tigris to Basra, where ships of the British Navy were waiting to take them the next 12,000 miles to England. Although the artist Cooper was not present on this occasion, he subsequently witnessed similar events, and would have been able to reconstruct the scene.

0c0afba6-5d14-5078-bcea-d6d65921461c.name: Passengers and onlookers waiting for the métropolitain at the Place de Bastille
0c0afba6-5d14-5078-bcea-d6d65921461c.second_name: Taken from *Vie et Métiers à Paris*
0c0afba6-5d14-5078-bcea-d6d65921461c.description2: Eugène Atget (1857–1927) began developing an interest in photography in 1888. He created his photos in series, and sold them to institutions. It was thus, that around 1898, he came to photograph the old neighbourhoods of Paris destined to demolition, and sold these photographs to the new Commission du Vieux Paris. As he photographed roads dug up by the urban excavations, he also captured onlookers fascinated by this new mode of transport. The Bastille station is pictured here, one of the overground sections of the ligne 1, which explains how these people were able to comfortably observe. The Colonne de Juillet of the Place de Bastille is visible in the background.

0c15121c-bdb4-5d29-91aa-079d86d55f11.name: Marseille: inauguration of M. Sanant's (Tunisia) exhibit - a picturesque corner of the West African pavilion
0c15121c-bdb4-5d29-91aa-079d86d55f11.description2: In the latter half of the 19th century, many European countries held exhibitions about their colonies, both during world fairs and smaller events. France used world fairs to "showcase" their colonies, both in the great Paris world fairs as well as smaller, colonial fairs organised in Marseille (1906, 1922) and Paris (1931). These expositions glorified colonial expansion, particularly by offering visitors an "object lesson". Tunisia took the spotlight in 1906 due to the central role it played in the ongoing dispute with Italy. The "indigenous villages", such as the one pictured in this photograph, were above all representations of the way Europeans imagined their colonies. They were later described as "human zoos" by historians of the late 20th century, due to the horrific practice of putting people for display as if they were animals.

0c19f7d6-2610-589f-a3df-5820477d393a.name: Captured arms (with accessories) from the occupation-campaign in Bosnia-Herzegovina 1878
0c19f7d6-2610-589f-a3df-5820477d393a.holder: Austrian Military Museum / Institute of Military History
0c19f7d6-2610-589f-a3df-5820477d393a.keywords: Pistols; Bosnia; arms; armours; metalwork; military objects; accessories; Ottoman Balkans; Ottoman amy; war; warfare
0c19f7d6-2610-589f-a3df-5820477d393a.description2: The 1878 Treaty of Berlin put the two Ottoman provinces of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the administration of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Between the 20th of July and the 29th of October 1878, the Austro-Hungarian Empire led a military campaign in those two provinces in order to establish its administration. During this armed conflict, several objects were taken, like a 16mm flintlock pistol with an Oriental-style snaphaunce lock (miquelet lock) entirely wrought from iron and richly decorated, showing as high a quality of craftsmanship as the accompanying gunpowder pourers, ramrods and bullet pouches.

0c2ced6e-dded-579f-8d98-8cd12c83980d.name: Bab Boujloud
0c2ced6e-dded-579f-8d98-8cd12c83980d.history: Bab Boujloud was built in the 12th century and has been restored and refurbished several times since. In 1913, during the reign of Sultan Mulay al-Hafiz, the gate was redecorated in glazed ceramic, blue on the side facing the Old *Medina* and green on the other side. The gate provides a monumental entrance to the square of the same name, west of the Old *Medina* of Fez.
0c2ced6e-dded-579f-8d98-8cd12c83980d.keywords: Portal; Moroccan city; traditional city; Islamic city; urban planning; national identity; traditional space; public space; urban space; plan; urban planning; geometrical motifs; Moroccan architects; Islamic art; Islamic architecture; Islamic influence; Islamic architecture in Morocco
0c2ced6e-dded-579f-8d98-8cd12c83980d.description2: This impressive 12th-century Gate, restored in 1912, is adorned with blue and green ceramic tiling bearing the name of the location. Beyond the aperture of the gate and around it, the landscape stretches over a vast, nearly flat, and irregular area. This area, surrounded by high adobe walls pierced with several doors, holds the prestigious Mulay Idris High School. Place Boujloud is in a strategic position of great cultural importance and very much animated by its popular character. The portal, admired for its fine interlacing ornamentation of blue and green, consists of a central arch and two smaller side arches that are in very good condition.

0c3d95fc-e6dc-5e76-8a44-96775f35c8c3.name: Hotel Kadri
0c3d95fc-e6dc-5e76-8a44-96775f35c8c3.description: Both the interior and exterior of the hotel are excellent examples Zahle's traditional stone architecture. It is one of the largest and most luxurious hotels in the city, and is frequently used by officials and dignitaries.
0c3d95fc-e6dc-5e76-8a44-96775f35c8c3.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
0c3d95fc-e6dc-5e76-8a44-96775f35c8c3.history: The Kadri Hotel was built in 1906, and has borne witness to much of the violence and turmoil in modern Lebanon. The hotel was taken over by the Ottoman army in 1914, who used it is a headquarters and hospital during World War I. It was later occupied by Syrian troops and sustained enormous damage. It was restored to its former glory following an extensive restoration project in the mid 90s. The hotel was briefly closed between February 2011 and 2013.
0c3d95fc-e6dc-5e76-8a44-96775f35c8c3.keywords: Kadri; Hotel; Zahle; Lebanon; Tourists; Tourism

0c5e1fe1-623d-5fde-b48c-d651eff7a4b0.name: House
0c5e1fe1-623d-5fde-b48c-d651eff7a4b0.dates: End of 19th – beginning of the 20th century
0c5e1fe1-623d-5fde-b48c-d651eff7a4b0.author: Prof. Petar Namichev (PhD)
0c5e1fe1-623d-5fde-b48c-d651eff7a4b0.history: The architectural concept of the 19th century "tower" house in Metochia and Montenegro influenced the development of spatial features of this type of house in Macedonia.
0c5e1fe1-623d-5fde-b48c-d651eff7a4b0.description2: The architecture of the Reka Area does not show many similar characteristics with neighbouring regions but shares common features with houses in some regions in Bulgaria, Albania, and elsewhere. This is a “tower” type of house. The entire three-storey house was built of stone. Thick and massive stone walls and very small windows on the ground floor were constructed for the purpose of safety in turbulent times, as well as for keeping heat inside during cold winters. The walls on the upper storey with slightly bigger windows were plated with wooden laths. The spatial organization of tower-houses in the Reka area share common features with Albanian tower houses regarding the commodity and defence security. The type of tower-house that used to be built in the Reka Area was the creation of the construction *tajfa* of Maksim Krstich.

0c62c358-069e-5101-ad0e-063173c5eefc.name: Chair
0c62c358-069e-5101-ad0e-063173c5eefc.description: This chair, known as *jamuga* in the Spanish tradition, is most certainly a Moresque European piece designed from a combination of pattern books. The chair consists of a great widely decorated back and a curved seat with two arms. The four legs are delicately ornamented. The inscriptions probably have been taken from a design book or other visual model too, rather than being designed by an Arab master calligrapher. The decorated panels, aesthetically pleasing, are imprecise in terms of execution and calligraphic style.
0c62c358-069e-5101-ad0e-063173c5eefc.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes, Cristina Giménez
0c62c358-069e-5101-ad0e-063173c5eefc.keywords: Production of applied arts in Europe in the Islamic mode; Orientalism

0c667bca-0934-5597-9606-a0052b8b5720.name: *Cairo, the Nile Dam*
0c667bca-0934-5597-9606-a0052b8b5720.second_name: Taken from Marcel Jusserand, *Souvenirs d'Egypte* (Memories of Egypt)
0c667bca-0934-5597-9606-a0052b8b5720.description2: The reign of Muhammad 'Ali Pasha was marked by a series of great changes, including attempts to take control of irrigation. The governor appointed French specialists, amongst whom was Linant de Bellefonds, and tasked them with the construction of a dam near Cairo. Linant de Bellefonds faced a great many difficulties during the construction, such as saving the pyramids, which the Pasha had wanted to destroy in order to supply the new dam with stone. The works were taken over by the engineer Eugène Mougel who added fortifications, as can be seen from this photograph, taken by a tourist at the beginning of the 20th century. The dam was completed c. 1835.
