a541b832-d774-57c4-adb6-f83fd670fffc.name: Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico “L. Pigorini” (National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography), Exhibition Room
a541b832-d774-57c4-adb6-f83fd670fffc.holder: National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography “Luigi Pigorini”
a541b832-d774-57c4-adb6-f83fd670fffc.author: Mario Mineo, Marina Minozzi
a541b832-d774-57c4-adb6-f83fd670fffc.keywords: Paleoethnology; archaeology; exploration; anthropology; natural history; material culture; academy; Jesuits; Egypt; Egyptology; collection; collector; exoticism; curiosities; wunderkammer; Museum Kircherianum; Baroque; languages; Arabic
a541b832-d774-57c4-adb6-f83fd670fffc.materials: Gelatine bromide negative impressed on glass plate
a541b832-d774-57c4-adb6-f83fd670fffc.third_name: Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico 'L. Pigorini', Sala Espositiva
a541b832-d774-57c4-adb6-f83fd670fffc.description2: The origins, in terms of scientific activity and conservation, of the Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico "Luigi Pigorini" in Rome, can be traced back to the foundation in 1875 of the “Regio Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico di Roma" (Royal National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography). Initially the museum was located in a wing of the Palazzo del Collegio Romano built in the late 16th century by the Society of Jesus. This rare image represents the old arrangement of one of the rooms of the Roman College, where the collection of antiquities and curiosities gathered together by Father Athanasius Kircher was kept after the foundation of the museum. According to the intentions of its founder, Luigi Pigorini, the purpose of this new institution was not only to gather together the remains of Italian prehistoric culture and the "primitive" cultures of other European and non-European peoples in a central museum located in the new capital of the Kingdom, but above all to support, promote and participate in research by palethnologists in Italy.

a565ef0e-9407-5de9-8ab2-05297761a4c9.name: *Amphitheatre at El Jem*
a565ef0e-9407-5de9-8ab2-05297761a4c9.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
a565ef0e-9407-5de9-8ab2-05297761a4c9.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
a565ef0e-9407-5de9-8ab2-05297761a4c9.archival: Copied from a drawinig by Sir Grenville Temple, published in his book The Shores and Islands of the Mediterranean in London in 1840, this drawing was taken from Chelli Zouhir, La Tunisie au Rythme des Estampes du XVe au XIXe siecle (Tunis, ed. Tunis Carthage: 1992), p. 65, fig. 25.
a565ef0e-9407-5de9-8ab2-05297761a4c9.description2: This drawing is by Sir Grenville Temple. The Amphitheatre of El Jem is seen as a symbol Roman Tunisia. Sometimes called the Colosseum of Ancient Thysdrus (El Jem), this amphiteatre is the only in the world, other than the colosseum of Rome, to have preserved all three of its tiers. Considered the most beautiful monument of ancient Africa, the Amphitheatre of El Jem was listed as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO on 26 October 1979.

a57a7875-1547-559b-a57d-6fa92bce59cf.name: Capsule-charge handgun
a57a7875-1547-559b-a57d-6fa92bce59cf.description: A capsule-charge gun called *Bou Habba* and crafted in southern Morocco in the early 19th century.

a57ada78-0cee-53e5-9161-c701a353df82.name: *The Coffee Shop*
a57ada78-0cee-53e5-9161-c701a353df82.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
a57ada78-0cee-53e5-9161-c701a353df82.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
a57ada78-0cee-53e5-9161-c701a353df82.description2: Coffee shops in the Near and Middle East were regular meeting places for men, who could while away hours chatting, playing domino, smoking and – crucially if dangerously – talking politics. In early 20th century Cairo as elsewhere, spedific cafes became important hubs for social and political discourse.This painting shows a traditional Near Eastern street café. Customers are sitting on long benches in front of its wooden openwork facade, A waiter with a red fez carries a brass coffee pot (dallah) and a tray. Behind him, through the wooden screen, the preparation area, in which the coffee is made, can just be seen on the left. A man wearing a white turban and blue gown, perhaps the proprietor, looks out on the right. All present are captivated by a carpet seller, who is standing in front of the cafe, offering up his wares.

a5ace29e-e1bf-5a09-9df7-66c7741b63b4.name: *Odalisque*
a5ace29e-e1bf-5a09-9df7-66c7741b63b4.keywords: Arts and Crafts; Daily utilitarian ware; Portugal; Vista Alegre; Factory; Orientalism
a5ace29e-e1bf-5a09-9df7-66c7741b63b4.description2: Sepia drawing representing odalisque, based on an epoch engraving. Painted by Joaquim José de Oliveira, Victor Rousseau’s disciple and master of painting and drawing of the Vista Alegre Factory, between 1869 and 1881.

a5b9fc7a-39f3-548a-ab66-613df1cdc6e7.name: Pendant for horses – Type 1
a5b9fc7a-39f3-548a-ab66-613df1cdc6e7.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
a5b9fc7a-39f3-548a-ab66-613df1cdc6e7.description2: This pendant was used on the horses of Ottoman officials and indicated their high status and wealth. It is made of a single, lozenge-shaped silver plaque decorated with red coral and blue gemstones. Silver leaf-shaped pendants dangle from this plaque and produce a tinkling noise when moving, announcing the arrival of the rider.

a5c93080-d37b-5926-ad79-2d9bb61932f2.name: *The Grand Bazaar*
a5c93080-d37b-5926-ad79-2d9bb61932f2.archival: Orientalist Paintings Collection-Suna and İnan Kıraç Foundation Collection
a5c93080-d37b-5926-ad79-2d9bb61932f2.description2: Amadeo Preziosi often presented genre scenes from Istanbul in his unique style. Specifically, he incorporated diverse scenes from the Bazaar in a number of his paintings. This venue, particular to Istanbul, has been of great interest to western artists, and in Edmondo De Amicis’s words “is not just a building but a town”. The Grand Bazaar, which housed shops for a wide range of commercial goods and catered to almost all of the needs of customers, offered an incredible visual richness and diversity to the western artist. A reflection of this opulence is also evident in Preziosi’s painting, which includes numerous details from daily life.

a5f9ccce-bdce-5ea9-8c27-06ad29d2353c.name: *Construction of a dam at Noisiel. State of the works on the 5th of August 1885*
a5f9ccce-bdce-5ea9-8c27-06ad29d2353c.artist: Photographer: Deraine and Auguste Hippolyte Collard
a5f9ccce-bdce-5ea9-8c27-06ad29d2353c.description2: Although little-known today, Auguste Hippolyte Collard (1812–1880s) contributed significantly to the rise of photography in France. He chose to specialise professionally in the photography of important construction sites. Thanks to him, today we can reconstruct the building of, for example, the Marne Dam at Noisiel in 1885. This dam is associated with the famous chocolatier Menier who became a pioneer in the field of cocoa refining, introducing the use of water power, among other new methods for the refinement of cocoa.

a61d424b-55c0-5f00-9818-9789ab7b964f.name: *North African woman washing*
a61d424b-55c0-5f00-9818-9789ab7b964f.archival: Berbrugger, *Algérie Historique Pittoresque et Monumentale*, Paris: J. Delahaye, 1843.
a61d424b-55c0-5f00-9818-9789ab7b964f.description2: The description online has a good explanation for Berbugger which could be used here.

a63d4087-1cd4-5ec4-b4ee-b445f990556b.name: *Chargeurs réunis. French steam-travel company (with destinations in South America)*
a63d4087-1cd4-5ec4-b4ee-b445f990556b.description2: At the end of the 19th century, France tried to catch up with its counterparts in the arms trade, as it had begun to fall behind England, Germany and others in recent decades. Commercial interests also played a part. In 1872, the Compagnie des Chargeurs Réunis established a maritime relationship between France and South America for the movement of passengers and merchandise. As this poster shows, they put great emphasis on the different services passengers were provided aboard these steamers.

a69264a8-566e-5e69-9661-65f4191695c9.name: Gold-embroidered, velvet Waistcoat
a69264a8-566e-5e69-9661-65f4191695c9.holder: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation / Sharjah Museums Department
a69264a8-566e-5e69-9661-65f4191695c9.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
a69264a8-566e-5e69-9661-65f4191695c9.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
a69264a8-566e-5e69-9661-65f4191695c9.description2: In the context of rising nationalisms, traditional costume played an important role, both in Europe and – to a lesser extent – in the Middle East.This long waistcoat is made of purple velvet with printed cotton lining. It carries extensive embroidery executed in gold-coloured metal thread, highlighting in particular the collar, the edges of the garment and the side pockets. Further ornamentation enhances the back. In the context of rising nationalisms, traditional costume played an important role, both in Europe and – to a lesser extent – in the Middle East. This waist coat may originally have been made in one of the European provinces of the Ottoman Empire, as it shows certain similarities with costume from the Balkans.

a6c96df7-d704-593e-8558-88a1905ae818.name: Musée d’Enfidha
a6c96df7-d704-593e-8558-88a1905ae818.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
a6c96df7-d704-593e-8558-88a1905ae818.history: From the first, this monument was built as both a church and a museum for Tunisia's ancient Christian art. Built in a neo-Roman style in the centre of Enfidha by European colonisers, this old church was consecrated to Saint Augustine, the patron saint of Roman Africa, on 1 May 1907. In 1964 the building, which had ceased to function as a church, was turned into a regional archaeological museum.
a6c96df7-d704-593e-8558-88a1905ae818.keywords: Architecture; Romano-Byzanine style; vaults; stained-glass windows; tapestry; marble
a6c96df7-d704-593e-8558-88a1905ae818.description2: The building, whose entrance sits underneath a clock tower, is built in the shape of a Latin cross, with an apse at the end where the choir can be found. The numerous important discoveries in the region in 1901 and 1905 encouraged the directors, the Archbishop of Carthage and the Société Franco-Africaine d’Enfidha to decorate the walls of the cathedral with an impressive series of Christian mosaics, all with a funerary or martyrologic theme. The museum houses an important collection of ancient ceramics. A number of pagan funerary or votive steles from local archaeological sites can also be found in the museum.

a6e38d56-3857-5b4e-a7be-06bb9cacae78.name: *The Petition Writer*
a6e38d56-3857-5b4e-a7be-06bb9cacae78.keywords: Painting; Osman Hamdi Bey; orientalist Turkish painters
a6e38d56-3857-5b4e-a7be-06bb9cacae78.description2: Osman Hamdi focused on dilemmas such as East and West, love and hate, life and death. While stylistically reminiscent of western Orientalist painters, his works reflect a more nuanced appreciation of Ottoman society and culture. He also gave importance to details while reflecting the colourful scenes of Turkish culture, traditional architecture, Ottoman fashion and domestic and social life of the women in the Ottoman Empire. And it’s obvious that he is the first painter who used human figures in the western style.

a6e39000-fe68-56fd-a598-f2bd48c41311.name: Silver brooch pin
a6e39000-fe68-56fd-a598-f2bd48c41311.description: The small collection of Berber jewellery that Sorolla´s family acquired during their visit to Morocco in February of 1919 includes this silver pin. The pins are indispensable parts of female jewellery; headbands, necklaces, bracelets and earrings complete the outfit. This pin served to fasten clothes to the shoulders and pins were always carried in pairs, connected by a string, which in this case was not preserved. The Museum preserves the other twin.
a6e39000-fe68-56fd-a598-f2bd48c41311.author: Covadonga Pitarch

a7135e6b-1b7e-5ddf-9568-b2daa5ac8d45.name: Louis Pasteur's work on silkworm illnesses. *Healthy Worms*
a7135e6b-1b7e-5ddf-9568-b2daa5ac8d45.description2: Silkworm farming developed in both France and Italy from the 15th century. Over-intensive farming caused the spread of various silkworm-based illnesses in the mid-19th century. Louis Pasteur, the famous scientist known for his work on the rabies vaccine amongst other things, was called on to find a cure. In 1870 he published *Une Étude sur la Maladie des Vers à Soie*, in which he proposed the use of various preventive methods, which proved effective. Pictured here is an illustration of silkworms immune to illness.

a73e56c5-c169-5488-aff8-8af1170f4be3.name: “The conqueror of Europe”
a73e56c5-c169-5488-aff8-8af1170f4be3.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
a73e56c5-c169-5488-aff8-8af1170f4be3.author: Giulia Barrera
a73e56c5-c169-5488-aff8-8af1170f4be3.second_name: A cartoon on the influenza pandemic of 1918, known as the “Spanish flu”
a73e56c5-c169-5488-aff8-8af1170f4be3.description2:
In Italy, the pandemic of influenza of 1918, known as “Spanish flu,” caused about 600,000 deaths out of a population of about 40 million. Around the world, it caused around 20 million deaths.  
The name derived from the fact that Spain – which did not participate in WWI – unlike other Western countries did not have press censorship, and so the news regarding the epidemic made headlines on newspapers. However, the epidemic did not start in Spain, but in China, then spread to the USA and arrived in Europe involuntarily carried by the US soldiers dispatched overseas.  
It hit particularly hard because the population was weakened by the hardships caused by the war and many medical doctors had been drafted, leaving civilians with insufficient medical assistance.
a73e56c5-c169-5488-aff8-8af1170f4be3.holding_institution_org: Biblioteca di Storia Moderna e Contemporanea

a77f3909-2307-52b5-b2aa-0229a50ed6c5.name: Ceiling
a77f3909-2307-52b5-b2aa-0229a50ed6c5.author: Houria Cherid

a7c102ce-f4bb-5330-8383-c17696408f62.name: Khayr al-Din Pacha
a7c102ce-f4bb-5330-8383-c17696408f62.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
a7c102ce-f4bb-5330-8383-c17696408f62.author: Bechir Yazidi
a7c102ce-f4bb-5330-8383-c17696408f62.description2: Khayr al-Din Pacha brought in many reforms which significantly changed the precolonial period, to a great extent Westernizing the Beylik of Tunis, which was later portrayed as "modernization". This Mamluk of circasian origin was probably born in 1825, and came to Tunis as a child in 1840. He quickly climbed the ranks and took his father-in-law Mustapha Khaznadar's place as Chief Minister under the rule of Mohamed Sadok Bey from 1873 to 1877. He died in 1890 in Istanbul, where he had served as grand vizier. He appears tall and majestic in this photograph, and carries authority in his piercing gaze. His jacket is richly decorated, bearing the coat of arms of the sovereign who bought him and brought him to Tunis, Ahmed Bey (1835–1855).

a7c58bbd-55c7-5749-907d-dcded54ad771.name: Tunisia at the 1867 Paris World Fair

a7c8b211-e332-5686-9c0a-beed901d97e7.keywords: Esposizione Internazionale di Roma; post-unitarian Italian society; nationalism; celebration of Ancient Rome; Roman empire; map; topography; reconstruction; model; exhibition building; exhibitions and urban spaces; archaeological findings in urban context

a7c8b211-e332-5686-9c0a-beed901d97e7.description2: On the occasion of the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911, the complex of the "Baths of Diocletian” was restored under the direction of the archeologist and topographer Rodolfo Lanciani. The site housed the Archaeological Exhibition dedicated to the Roman culture in the Imperial Era with a particular interest for its positive influence on the "ex provinces”. Every single nation participated through original reproductions of archaeological materials, often lost. The photo shows archaeological materials and casts displayed in the room dedicated to Austria.

a7ce06ce-7dc4-5296-b742-d917fdbbf2c7.name: 'Casa del Mar' Fortress
a7ce06ce-7dc4-5296-b742-d917fdbbf2c7.history: Tarfaya became a British airmail postal centre in 1882. In 1889, Scottish entrepreneur Donald Mackenzie persuaded the head of Sous, Muhammad Bayruk, to allow him to establish a trading post on Tarfaya strip (also known as Cape Juby strip), which was about three kilometres wide by 12 km long. Mackenzie built the factory/trading post and named it Port Victoria, which he managed through his own North-West Africa Company. Under the Spanish Protectorate the name was changed to Casa Del Mar (House of the Sea).
a7ce06ce-7dc4-5296-b742-d917fdbbf2c7.keywords: Caravan; caravan routes; trade; economy; commerce; port; traditional port; sea routes; maritime routes; traditional routes; trading hubs; trading route; strategical port; strategical hub; modernisation; industrialisation; Moroccan ports; Islamic city; changes in urban space; Moroccan city; foreign companies; Nort West Africa; British in Morocco; postal services; British postal service; factory; industrialists; industrial architecture; military architecture; British architects; British architects in Morocco; fortress; Spanish in Morocco
a7ce06ce-7dc4-5296-b742-d917fdbbf2c7.description2: At the end of the 19th century, Scottish entrepreneur Donald Mackenzie persuaded the Governor of Sous, Muhammad Bayruk, to cede him a strip of land roughly three kilometres wide and 12km long on which to establish a trading post. It was known as Tarfaya strip or the Cape Juby strip. On it, Mackenzie built Port Victoria, a trading post/factory, which he managed through his own North-West Africa Company, hoping to capture a portion of the caravan trade. The reinforced stone buttressed building of two floors covers an area of 1,200m².

a7d32c3d-fe87-5afb-b350-091e02c5d6d1.name: Pendant
a7d32c3d-fe87-5afb-b350-091e02c5d6d1.holder: National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography “Luigi Pigorini”
a7d32c3d-fe87-5afb-b350-091e02c5d6d1.author: Marina Minozzi
a7d32c3d-fe87-5afb-b350-091e02c5d6d1.keywords: Egyptomania; Gaetano Rosellini; university; collector; photograph; anthropology; palaeoethnology; material culture; Florence; Pisa; Egyptology; Nubia; languages; hieroglyph; William Matthew Flinders Petrie; Jacques de Morgan; David Randall-MacIver
a7d32c3d-fe87-5afb-b350-091e02c5d6d1.description2: This ivory tooth-shaped amulet, decorated with a series of diagonal parallel lines, comes from the excavations conducted between 1900 to 1901 by David Randall-MacIver and Luigi Pigorini. As a result of earlier excavations by W. Petrie and J. De Morgan, who documented the existence of an era preceding the 1st dynasty, Pigorini, an archaeologist and the director of the "Museo Preistorico Etnografico e Kircheriano", decided to increase the museum’s Egyptian archaeological collection. In 1878 he began to acquire important groups, but the main body of the collection was donated by Randall-MacIver in 1901, from excavations he carried out on the behalf of the Egypt Exploration Fund in the town of el-Amrah, Upper Egypt. Another major purchase — from the Italian Archaeological Mission in Egypt (excavations of Hammamiye) led by Ernesto Schiaparelli, director of the Egyptian Museum in Turin — followed in 1905.  The last main acquisition took place in 1913 when the Egyptian objects from Enrico Hillyer Giglioli’s collection entered the museum collection.

en: Cappozzo, M., “La collezione egizia del Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico ‘Luigi Pigorini’”, in *Bullettino di Paletnologia Italiana*, Roma, Istituto Poligrafico e Zecca dello Stato, (2005–2007), 96: 131–202, cat. 73.

a7f5c0c6-53c4-5240-ae78-34f4ac89dbbc.name: Medal of the World Trade Fair in Vienna
a7f5c0c6-53c4-5240-ae78-34f4ac89dbbc.keywords: Emperor Franz Joseph; World Trade Fair Vienna; numismatics
a7f5c0c6-53c4-5240-ae78-34f4ac89dbbc.description2: The medal shows Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom. The opposite side of the medal shows the pavilion of the 1873 World's Fair in Vienna, above it two griffons hold a shield with the initials of Emperor Franz Joseph crowned by the crown of Austria.

a7fd98fa-f450-5ba3-b6d2-3909a56326ac.name: Decorated panel featuring a mosque
a7fd98fa-f450-5ba3-b6d2-3909a56326ac.description2: An Ottoman-style mosque, identifiable by its cone-shaped minarets, sits in the middle of this horseshoe arch supported by two columns. The lower panel contains a vase with various flowers emerging from it, such as carnations, tulips, and vine leaves. A dense rinceau pattern with flowers and leaves fills the gaps in the arch and the keystone and decorates the capitals of the columns. The main colours are yellow green and blue, although beige and brown also feature. This item shows traces of both Ottoman and Andalusian influences.

a81b5a25-c516-56c6-b670-eb0ae21f4f03.name: The Moorish Banqueting hall (Wilhelma Park)
a81b5a25-c516-56c6-b670-eb0ae21f4f03.holder: Wilhelma, Zoological and Botanical Garden Stuttgart
a81b5a25-c516-56c6-b670-eb0ae21f4f03.history:
King Wilhelm I of Württemberg commissioned to Karl Ludwig von Zanth in 1837 the design of Moorish style buildings for his Wilhelma garden. The architect planned and built all the buildings with the exception of the Damascene Hall.  
The idea was not to reproduce faithfully the Islamic art but to lend an “oriental” flair to the garden. The mention of an “oriental garden” conjured up visions of elegance, luxury, colourful brilliance, seduction and eroticism.  
The Moorish style recalls the Islamic art of Spain and North Africa between the 12th and 15th centuries which reached its zenith in the Alhambra. It was fashionable in 19th century: Wilhelma is also known as the “Alhambra on the river Neckar” and other buildings – synagogues in Berlin and Vienna for example – were built in the Moorish style.
a81b5a25-c516-56c6-b670-eb0ae21f4f03.description2:
The Moorish Banqueting Hall was built in 1851 as a place for royal festivities, receptions and balls. The Moorish Villa and Moorish Banqueting Hall were separated by the Moorish Garden and linked to each other by the Covered Walkway.  
Amongst the absolute social highlights were the Stuttgart Imperial Days in September 1853. King Wilhelm I of Württemberg had invited Tsar Alexander II and the French Emperor Napoleon III to a meeting of reconciliation at Wilhelma. In 1944 the Moorish Banqueting Hall was heavily damaged by bombing. In 1961, after much deliberation – controversial as the decision was – the remains were demolished. Today the Aquarium with the Crocodile Hall is standing at the site. One small section of the original façade has survived. It forms the wall at the side of the Aquarium facing the Water Lily Pond.

a848f65f-c1fe-59d4-94f0-740ada4365f3.name: *Part of the* Via Dolorosa
a848f65f-c1fe-59d4-94f0-740ada4365f3.author: Maria Francesca Carvelli (MWNF)
a848f65f-c1fe-59d4-94f0-740ada4365f3.archival: Johnstone, Catherine Laura, *Christian and Jewish Pilgrims to the Holy Land*, London, 1899
a848f65f-c1fe-59d4-94f0-740ada4365f3.keywords: Pilgrimage; pilgrims; Christian pilgrimage; Jewish pilgrimage; Palestine; Holy Land; Jerusalem; sacred places; travel; travel book; Ottoman Palestine; local Jewish community
a848f65f-c1fe-59d4-94f0-740ada4365f3.description2: This photograph shows the Via Dolorosa in Jerusalem as it appeared in 1899. It was a typical destination for Christian pilgrims travelling from Europe and Russia. Christian pilgrimage was seen in many cases as a starting point to describe "exotic" places and the "Eastern" culture. Some Christian pilgrims described in their writings historical and cultural details and curiosities and their impressions of 19th century Palestinian society, the increasing number of pilgrims – especially Russian and Jews – and the institutions such as the Russian consulate, English and German churches and Latin monks that accommodated the Christian pilgrims.

a8683bd7-cbf6-5821-a911-6ea63acae710.name: The Khaldouniya
a8683bd7-cbf6-5821-a911-6ea63acae710.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
a8683bd7-cbf6-5821-a911-6ea63acae710.author: Bechir Yazidi
a8683bd7-cbf6-5821-a911-6ea63acae710.description2: Founded in Tunis on 22 December 1896, this school can be best described as a sort of modern school. Today, it houses a bilingual library holding several thousand volumes and hundreds of manuscripts, attached to the Bibliothèque Nationale de Tunisie. Founded by the Young Tunisians (Harakat al-Shabab al-Tunisi) and directed by Béchir Sfar, the school's name is a direct reference to the great Arab thinker Ibn Khaldoun. It had the aim of disseminating scientific and practical knowledge in the Arab cultural sphere, particularly among the students of the Zaytuna Mosque, whose teachings were considered archaic and purely religious. The institution was built near the Zaytuna thanks to the support of the French Resident-General, René Millet, who drew up its regulations and in so doing notably failed to include political and religious discussions, choosing instead to focus on encouraging critical and reflective thinking.

a8732393-9f73-5349-bf08-2e06bf17b6f1.name: Jar with animal decorations
a8732393-9f73-5349-bf08-2e06bf17b6f1.description2: This oval-shaped double-handled *charbiya* has a long neck, a curved rim and a flat bottom. The main colours of the decorations are yellow, green and brown. On the shoulders, a strip of leaves in green and yellow are superimposed on a paler green background. A second strip of brown herringbone sits above a yellow and brown spotted cheetah, painted in profile with its head turned in full face and its big green eyes wide open. Its back is raised and topped with a ribbed crest. This item shows traces of both Ottoman and Andalusian influences.

a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.name: Decanter (one of a set of three)
a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.type: Furniture and decorative objects; vessel; glasswork
a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.holder: Shangri La, Doris Duke Foundation for Islamic Art
a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.provenance: Europe, made for export to Iran
a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.keywords: decanter; glass; beads; decoupage; Qajar; Nasr al-Din Shah; Europe; portrait
a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.description2: During the nineteenth century, European centres of glass production, particularly those in France and Bohemia, created Islamic-style works of art to be exported to countries like Egypt, Syria, Iran, and India. The DDFIA collection includes several examples of such European glass. This bottle – one in a set of three – was certainly produced for an Iranian recipient, for it features portraits of the Qajar shah Nasr al-Din (r. 1848–96). Purchased in 1959.

a8f4d9df-4a01-55fb-98f5-9b27f994af97.description2: To travel with «quina» – cinchona plant – to the non European territories was really mandatory for health reasons, specially to attack malaria disease.

a9007630-d81f-5724-87ad-6fc202c954e3.name: Gufas (Quffas) on the Tigris at Baghdad
a9007630-d81f-5724-87ad-6fc202c954e3.description2: This stereoview by the Keystone company (a reprint from an older negative) was part of a popular box-set of images about Mesopotamia. They were sold across Europe. The text on the reverse contains description of the geography, architecture (explanation of minarets, lament at the absence of fine buildings through devastation of the city by fire, habit of wealthy to live in unpretentious houses to avoid the attention of the Turkish taxman) and history, plus brief caption in half a dozen languages.

a901418e-d33a-5654-af66-ca933582dfb2.name: The actress Carolina Ungher in the role of Anne Boleyn in Donizetti's Opera *Anna Bolena*
a901418e-d33a-5654-af66-ca933582dfb2.archival: AS Reggio Emilia, Archivi Teatrali, Archivio Vivi, Ritratti di maestri e artisti di canto prosa e ballo che agirono nei teatri di Reggio, sec. XVIII-XIX

a91be56f-fdaa-598c-a438-db2d0512a2e7.name: *Athenian Bride*
a91be56f-fdaa-598c-a438-db2d0512a2e7.author: Tsigakou, The Rediscovery of Greece, p.191
a91be56f-fdaa-598c-a438-db2d0512a2e7.description2: Louis Dupré (1789–1837) visited Greece in 1819. He exhibited Greek subjects at the Salons of 1827, 1831, 1833 and 1855. In 1825 he published a set of colored lithographs of views and studies of costumes from Greece, entitled *Voyages à Athènes et Constantinople*. Dupré recorded his experiences of travel in the Levant in 1819 mainly through portraits of the people he met. In addition to the lithographs in this book, Dupré also produced loose broadsheet lithographed plates. Many of these are in the possession of the Cabinet des Estampes of the Bibliothèque Nationale. Much has been written on Dupré. *Athenian Bride* depicts the preparations of an Athenian wedding. The bride patiently waits as the groom is ritually shaved.

en: Tsigakou, Fani-Maria, *The Rediscovery of Greece: Travellers and Painters of the Romantic Era*, London: Thames & Hudson, 1981.

a9281dfb-f5ce-5f06-9747-94bf00a2f99e.name: Shield
a9281dfb-f5ce-5f06-9747-94bf00a2f99e.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
a9281dfb-f5ce-5f06-9747-94bf00a2f99e.keywords: Military object; Metalwork; Cast steel; Arms and armour; Shield
a9281dfb-f5ce-5f06-9747-94bf00a2f99e.description2: These shields were used by the Ottoman soldiers in Lebanon in the 19th century to quash resistance movements. As the Lebanese resistance had no weapons of their own, the fighters frequently ambushed Ottoman soldiers and took their weapons. This shield is an example of such weaponry, which was taken by the resistance and used against the Ottomans. It was used mainly by foot soldiers, and was hand-held with straps going around the wearer's arm. Although ineffective against newer weaponry such as guns, the shield was used by soldiers to deflect arrows or swords. It is made of cast steel, with no decorative elements of notes. It features four bosses and reverse arm fixings.

a9297ffd-8462-5dd7-8571-a2309301164e.name: Egypt. Mummies found in the kings' tomb in Thebes
a9297ffd-8462-5dd7-8571-a2309301164e.second_name: Taken from *Grèce, Egypte, Palestine.* Photographies Bonfils
a9297ffd-8462-5dd7-8571-a2309301164e.description2: Félix Bonfils settled as a photographer in Libya in 1867. Helped by his assistants, he reproduced photographs taken during his travels in neighbouring countries. These pictures were sold in albums or individually, to tourists or painters exploring the Middle East. In this photograph a merchant of Thebes is pictured, napping amongst the mummies he sells. The mummies were then bought either by European collectors, or for other purposes (medical ingredients, etc.).

a946e99a-c0f3-5d45-9fb0-6eec1cfb9b75.name: The cutting of granite blocks for the construction of the first dam on the Nile. Many Italian stonecutters participated in the works
a946e99a-c0f3-5d45-9fb0-6eec1cfb9b75.author: Patrizia Pampana
a946e99a-c0f3-5d45-9fb0-6eec1cfb9b75.description2: In the year 1900, Count Giulio d’Aspremont (an Italian diplomat), visited the construction site of the first dam across the Nile (today known as the Aswan Low Dam or Old Aswan Dam). He took several photographs of the works and of the monuments on the island of Philae that were slate to be submerged by the water. He published some of them on the *Bulletin of the Italian Geographical Society*, where he wrote that up to 2,000 Italian workers were employed in the works (as stone-cutters, miners and masons), out of a total labour force of about 10,000 or 12,000; an Italian village had sprung up on the Nile banks, with modest little houses, trattorias and shops.

a9495bdc-29e8-5ac4-be85-88883d1f30cd.name: *Madame Josephine the Landlady of the Hotel Constantinople in a Turkish Dress*
a9495bdc-29e8-5ac4-be85-88883d1f30cd.keywords: hotel; women; fashion; costume; Orientalism; travel; traveller
a9495bdc-29e8-5ac4-be85-88883d1f30cd.description2: From Sir David Wilkie's *Sketches in Turkey, Syria & Egypt*, 1840 & 1841. Shows what would have been a familiar to face to many travellers.

a94b6245-85b8-5f79-b98e-7c8a3c4249f7.name: Italian colonial soldiers (known as '*askari*') wounded in the battle of Maharuga (Tripolitania, Libya) receiving assistance
a94b6245-85b8-5f79-b98e-7c8a3c4249f7.holder: Italian Institute for African and Oriental Studies
a94b6245-85b8-5f79-b98e-7c8a3c4249f7.author: Giulia Barrera
a94b6245-85b8-5f79-b98e-7c8a3c4249f7.description2:
In this photo one can see African soldiers (presumably Eritrean) of the Italian colonial army. Italy used Eritrea foremost as a source of *askari* (soldiers) who were made to fight for Italy’s colonial conquests in Somalia, Libya and Ethiopia.  
Today, Eritrean migrants who traverse Libya report that they perceive a special hostility against them, because Libyans remember that Eritreans served in the Italian colonial army.
a94b6245-85b8-5f79-b98e-7c8a3c4249f7.holding_institution_org: Istituto italiano per l'Africa e l'Oriente

a95aa12b-08ad-5216-93c1-8009226cdb57.name: Saint-Cyprien. Combine harvesters and sheaf binders on the road.
a95aa12b-08ad-5216-93c1-8009226cdb57.second_name: Société des Fermes Françaises de Tunisie
a95aa12b-08ad-5216-93c1-8009226cdb57.description2: French agriculture in Tunisia began either through the establishment of large properties by private initiatives, or the introduction of settlers by the public authorities. This is a photograph from the "first phase" - one of the "companies" (of "French farms") had purchased a large plot of land, and employed a number of (largely Arab and Italian) workers to cultivate the land. It shows two combine harvesters which had been imported for the development of intensive cereal faming, and would have been used as advertising for Europeans considering investing in this type of agricultural "company".

a95b3b6a-66a7-5a79-99bd-6be598fec282.name: Dolmabahçe Palace Theatre under construction
a95b3b6a-66a7-5a79-99bd-6be598fec282.author: Bahattin Öztuncay
a95b3b6a-66a7-5a79-99bd-6be598fec282.description2: James Robertson came to Istanbul in 1841 to assist with modernization of the Imperial Mint and remained for 40 years, during which he served without interruption under no less than four Ottoman sultans. He started as head etcher in the Ottoman Mint. Then he began to take photos of Istanbul. He also painted watercolours, and in the early 1850s became interested in photography and went on to become a leading name among early photographers. Robertson’s Istanbul photographs are concerned primarily with the city’s historical monuments. They reveal the city’s magnificent Byzantine and Ottoman structures from different angles and with close-ups taken in an approach that is usually quite aesthetic. In this photo, Dolmabahçe Palace Theatre is seen under construction.

a967717f-9e55-5ff9-83cb-584a32659274.name: Gheorghe Tattarescu – Portrait of Nicolae Bălcescu

a96d4c0a-5e74-5015-a893-8254aa4f6dbd.name: Quranic school
a96d4c0a-5e74-5015-a893-8254aa4f6dbd.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
a96d4c0a-5e74-5015-a893-8254aa4f6dbd.description2: Pictured here is a school using traditional teaching methods - a Quranic school or a *kouttab*. The students are seated in a circle on mats on the floor of a sparsely decorated room around their teacher, the *moueddeb*. In the 19th century and early 20th centuries, the Quranic schools were a fundamental part of traditional education, where students would learn the Quran, Islamic thought and the basic rules of the Arabic language.

a98c40f6-a4df-55c5-b720-2e843d2d4af6.name: General view of the excavations in the crypt of the Saint-Geneviève monastery, in 1807.
a98c40f6-a4df-55c5-b720-2e843d2d4af6.description2: Although only the library remains today, in the 18th century there used to be a great monasterial complex - the Abbey of Sainte-Geneviève - next to the Church of Saint-Etienne du Mont in Paris. The monastery was destroyed to make space for the construction of the Panthéon and Rue Clovis. The architect Bourla, who was tasked with its demolition, made a great number of sketches and organized many excavations in the crypt, where a number of sarcophagi were discovered. His son Alexandre, who had helped out on the site as a child, worked on the drawings that illustrated the archaeological reports.

ab21cc92-59d1-559f-ab5b-149da55c95bd.description2: In 1891 Sultan Abdülhamid II founded the Yıldız Çini Fabrika-i Hümâyûnu (Yıldız Royal Tile Factory) in the garden of Yıldız Palace for the purpose of reviving Turkish tile art and giving it a new direction and momentum. Vases, hanging wall plates and many sorts of daily-use wares were produced in the factory, including writing and dinner table utensils, card plates, lidded bowls, pans, *aşure* (a kind of dessert) trays, sugar bowls, tea and coffee cups. A vase with conical body with wide mouth and round foot. There is a landscape painted on its body. The rest of its body has an intricate floral design painted on a green base. On the base a stamp of the star and crescent and dates of 1312-13 written in Arabic can be seen.

ac213e50-9aa9-50fe-a88f-16a3840fbce1.name: *Departure of a Caravan to Mecca from Bab el-Nasr Gate, Cairo*
ac213e50-9aa9-50fe-a88f-16a3840fbce1.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority
ac213e50-9aa9-50fe-a88f-16a3840fbce1.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
ac213e50-9aa9-50fe-a88f-16a3840fbce1.description2: Traditionally, most Muslim pilgrims went to Makkah on foot as part of a caravan. Cairo was one of the most important starting points for pilgrim caravans, particularly as it dispatched the ceremonial Mahmal, an ornamental litter containing a Qur’an manuscript and ritual hangings for the Holy Places. Traditionally, the Hajj caravan left the city from the Bab al Nasr gate. In order to ensure the caravan's smooth progression, the Amir al-Hajj organised each section and allocated it its correct place within the sequence. The caravan was headed up by bedouin guides, followed by water carriers and important officials. Next came the treasury and precious gifts intended for the Holy Places, carefully shielded by the ruler's special guards and soldiers. Another, well-protected treasury section - this one intended for the upkeep of the caravan itself - followed and, behind it, a numerous array of traders and merchants. The rest of the caravan was made up of the actual pilgrims from all over the region.

ac262d55-b70d-52be-a08e-76b8060b08ee.name: *Khalid ibn al-Walid Mosque*
ac262d55-b70d-52be-a08e-76b8060b08ee.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
ac262d55-b70d-52be-a08e-76b8060b08ee.author: Stefan Weber
ac262d55-b70d-52be-a08e-76b8060b08ee.second_name: View of the mosque in classical Ottoman revival style from the courtyard
ac262d55-b70d-52be-a08e-76b8060b08ee.description2: This Mosque, built in the early 20th century, was dedicated to Khalid ibn al-Walid, the national hero who conquered Syria for Islam in AD 636. Most of the interior consists out of a single large prayer hall, which contains the domed mausoleum of Khalid ibn al-Walid. It shows over 50 battles he victoriously commanded. The mosque exemplifies the Ottoman architectural style; particularly beautiful are the minarets out of white limestone and the opulent décor inside. Since 2011, the mosque has been a focal point for political opponents protesting against the Syrian government and was damaged.

ac5b0f5f-98d9-556f-869d-b17cc4a654a2.name: *The Gate of the Roman*
ac5b0f5f-98d9-556f-869d-b17cc4a654a2.author: Athens 1985, no 205 (F-M Tsigakou)
ac5b0f5f-98d9-556f-869d-b17cc4a654a2.artist: Théodore Achille Louis, Vicomte du Moncel
ac5b0f5f-98d9-556f-869d-b17cc4a654a2.description2: Since King Otto (1833–1863) made efforts to transform immediately ruinous Athens into a European capital worthy of its erstwhile glory, around the mid-nineteenth century spectacular changes were made in the urban planning structure and morphology of the city. A reliable image of Athens at this time is given by Du Moncel in his book *Vues pittoresques des monuments d’Athenes*. This particular representation of Athens is the Roman Agora (Forum Romanum), natural continuation of the ancient Agora, was built c.10BC, the Gate of Athena Archegetis, which is depicted here. In Ottoman times this Roman gate was known as the Pazaroporta (Bazaar Gate), because it was used as the entrance to the bazaar, the commercial centre of Athens, which occupied the area between the Roman Agora and the Library of Hadrian.

en: Tsigakou, Fani-Maria, *British Images of Greece from the Benaki Museum Collections*, Athens: Benaki Museum, 1995.

acb1417e-ded5-525f-a850-94113fa99185.name: Musée de Carthage
acb1417e-ded5-525f-a850-94113fa99185.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
acb1417e-ded5-525f-a850-94113fa99185.history: The museum was founded in 1875 on the premises of the Pères Blancs seminary, on the Byrsa Hill near the Saint-Louis Cathedral in Carthage. It was called the Musée Saint-Louis until 1899, and the Musée Lavigerie until 1956. It was given its current name by the Tunisian government following independence and the signing of the Modus Vivendi with the Catholic Church in 1964, at which point they relinquished all rights to the land.
acb1417e-ded5-525f-a850-94113fa99185.description2: The Musée de Carthage houses some of the most beautiful items from the Roman and Punic eras discovered on the Carthage archaeological site since the 19th century. After a long period of restoration, the museum also took on the findings from the UNESCO 1972–75 international arcehological campaign. It offered a new museographic approach, with each of the building's renovated rooms looking onto the beautiful landscape of Tunis Bay. The museum is thematically organised, with rooms dedicated to sculpture, amphoras, mosaics, or rooms reserved especially for works discovered by specific archaeological campaigns on the site.

acc57934-ae32-5e43-8f31-305447337577.description2: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. Cendere Hamidian Water Pump Station was built by Abdülhamid II in 1902 at an altitude of 34 metres above sea level. With its function, architectural design and mechanical equipment, the station is a unique monument to the history of the architecture industry in the Ottoman Empire. It pumped to Balmumcu and Beşiktaş – in the direction of Tophane, moving water coming from 20 different pipes in Kağıthane using steam pump machines.

ad246261-371b-52ce-a11b-7790d61625de.description2: The first fort at Sharjah town was destroyed by the British in 1819-20. Under Shaikh Sultan bin Saqr II al-Qasimi a new fort was built 1823/4. From sources we can assume that the original fort was of traditional square one-storey design with tall corner towers and an inner courtyard. Its most unusual element was the design of its al-Mhalousa tower, *mhalous* meaning 'twisted' in Arabic. Originally, Sharjah's fort, known as *al-Hisn*, was built onto the desert side of the previously existing town wall and incorporated a round tower known as *al-Kabs*. The fort served as the residence of the ruling Qasimi family until the early 14th/20th century. In 1970 it was partially demolished to make way for urban development, but several key parts, including the so-called *al-Kabs* tower on its northwestern side, survived. The current fort – a reconstruction and a museum – stands as a reminder to an important building of crucial importance to Sharjah's history, witnessing key political, social, commercial and military events in its history.

adb3e161-8b56-5dcf-80b9-dddd0fdde32d.author: Maria Francesca Carvelli (MWNF)
adb3e161-8b56-5dcf-80b9-dddd0fdde32d.archival: Johnstone, Catherine Laura, *Christian and Jewish Pilgrims to the Holy Land*, London, 1899
adb3e161-8b56-5dcf-80b9-dddd0fdde32d.keywords: Pilgrimage; pilgrims; Christian pilgrimage; Jewish pilgrimage; Palestine; Holy Land; Jerusalem; sacred places; travel; travel book; Ottoman Palestine; local Jewish community
adb3e161-8b56-5dcf-80b9-dddd0fdde32d.description2: This drawing shows the chapel as it appeared in 1899. It was a typical destination for Christian pilgrims travelling from Europe and Russia. Christian pilgrimage was often seen as a starting point to describe "exotic" places and the "Eastern" culture. Some Christian pilgrims described in their writings historical and cultural details and curiosities and their impressions of 19th century Palestinian society, the increasing number of pilgrims – especially Russian and Jews – and the institutions such as the Russian consulate, English and German churches and Latin monks that accommodated the Christian pilgrims.

ae264026-52c5-575e-8918-d09df5811c0b.name: Quinta da Regaleira
ae264026-52c5-575e-8918-d09df5811c0b.type: Palace and Gardens; Unesco Cultural Heritage Classification
ae264026-52c5-575e-8918-d09df5811c0b.holder: Sintra Parks Monte da Lua, Conservation Company
ae264026-52c5-575e-8918-d09df5811c0b.history:
António Augusto Carvalho Monteiro (1848–1920) assisted by Italian architect Luigi Manini conceived The Garden of Quinta da Regaleira as a sacred and symbolic space,  
inspired by the Garden of the Desert de Retz in Marly; Torrigiani Garden in Florence amongst others. The choice of its location in Sintra, in the Monte da Lua, was relevant as a sacred site since the Neolithic, associated with legends and rituals of underground worlds.  
Carvalho Monteiro as a Mason filled his home with various symbolic references namely Christian, pagan, Neo - Templars and classical literature as Dante\`s Divine Comedy. The visiting trail, beyond the ludic aspect aims to recreate the theme of “death and resurrection” like the descent to the darkness before returning to the light.
ae264026-52c5-575e-8918-d09df5811c0b.keywords: Neomanueline; Romanticism; Nature; Garden; Spirituality; Mistery; Alchemy
ae264026-52c5-575e-8918-d09df5811c0b.architects: António Carvalho Monteiro (1848–1920); architect Luigi Manini (1848–1936)
ae264026-52c5-575e-8918-d09df5811c0b.description2: A man of inquiring scientific mind and vast culture, Carvalho Monteiro left imprinted in stone his cosmological vision, a synthesis of the spiritual memory of mankind stemmed in the Portuguese Mythical Tradition.  The art and architecture of the mansion and the chapel, built in neo-Manueline style, were conjugated with other buildings in the bosom of an Edenic garden. A “Philosopher's Dwelling” par excellence, conveying a message adressed to those who are are fit to engage in the Adventure of self-knowledge, Quinta da Regaleira emerges from the Sintra Cultural Landscape as an example of the Total Oeuvre and as expression of a new mythical territory, where Philosophy, Art and Nature come together.

ae42a45e-443f-5a1d-aaab-85cd72bce06d.name: *A Greek Mountaineer*
ae42a45e-443f-5a1d-aaab-85cd72bce06d.author: Washington, D.C., 1991, 80-81, no 28
ae42a45e-443f-5a1d-aaab-85cd72bce06d.description2: During the Ottoman occupation, Greek peasants who were dispossessed of their property often retreated to impregnable mountain regions, where they engaged in resistance against the Turks. These mountaineers, who both fascinated and frightened European travellers, were romanticised by artists and poets such as Lord Byron. The man depicted here clearly represents the type of mountaineer described by Byron. To emphasize his costume and his swift movement, he appears in full gear, the sleeves of his jacket falling freely to the back as if to underscore his impulsive gesture. Pistols and knives are tucked in his belt. His right hand rests on his musket; his left hand proudly touches the tip of his sword. Haag chose to place the figure in a grand mountainous landscape, complete with a ruined temple. This sacred monument may be identified as the temple of Apollo Epicurius in Arcadia in the central Peloponnese. This enhances the dignity of the figure, whose nobility and heroism are worthy of the principles of his legendary ancestors.

ae4f06c1-8888-5c57-81c6-70d929b50897.name: *Nişan-ı Maarif* (Badge of Education)
ae4f06c1-8888-5c57-81c6-70d929b50897.description2: The owner of this medallion was Dr. Mustafa Münif Pasha (1855-1937), who was the founder and director of the Turkish School of Pharmacy, Dentistry, Midwives and Nurses. He worked as an assistant in the anatomy department starting in 1881. Later, he gave classes on surgery. In 1886 he gave courses on midwifery. This medallion (*Nişan- Maarif*) was given to teachers who were successful in science and art. On the front of the medallion, on the left there are olive tree leaves enamelled in green and yellow while on the right we see oak leaves. Those two forms a crescent on top for the ribbon. On the lower part the leaves merge with a pink ribbon pattern. In the middle of the medallion there is a *tuğra* of Mehmed Reşad V. (1909–1918) on red enamelled background. Around the *tuğra* (monogram) there is an inscription that reads, “*ulûm ve fünûn ve sanayi'-i nefîse*” (sciences and knowledge and fine arts).

ae85f44d-6a24-58d0-81d8-1e9715c81ac8.name: Colonial style building
ae85f44d-6a24-58d0-81d8-1e9715c81ac8.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
ae85f44d-6a24-58d0-81d8-1e9715c81ac8.history: In Tunis, the capital of the Protectorate imposed by France on Tunisia in 1881, the European quarter built itself right next to the old Arab medina. A new kind of home - the investment property - soon appeared, and the term balas (from the Italian *palazzo*) became widespread. These two or three-storey housing blocks greatly affected the city's urban landscape by introducing many different architectural styles as well as new architects, designers and builders with from different backgrounds. The 19th century was the century of eclecticism in Tunisia (both neo-classical and neo-baroque), whereas the 20th century was most marked by the influence of Art Nouveau.
ae85f44d-6a24-58d0-81d8-1e9715c81ac8.keywords: Art Nouveau; colonial style; eclecticism; Neo-Baroque
ae85f44d-6a24-58d0-81d8-1e9715c81ac8.description2: 114 Rue de Yougoslavie, the former French Embassy and General Residence previously known as the Disegni building, was designed by the famous architect Auguste Peters, who remains a leading figure of eclecticism. The finely carved balconies, ribbed stone corbels, delicate Venetian style mouldings, overhanging arches and columned galleries all add to the building's majestic character. Auguste Peters was a great master of eclecticism in the first decade of the 20th century, and decorative elements like these characterise his work.

ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.name: *Suq al-Hamidiyya, Damascus*
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.author: Stefan Weber
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.second_name: Covered market constructed in the shape of an arcade turning it to the worldwide longest arcade of the fin de siecle
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.description2: The Suq al-Hamidiyya, built in 1886 and 1894, is by far the biggest and most famous suq in Damascus. This bazaar street also links the two most important historic buildings, the Umayyad Mosque and the Citadel. It was built along its western section by incorporating earlier structures, whereas the eastern part of the street was a completely new construction cutting through the existing buildings. The commercial thoroughfare is 450 metres long and 8.70 to 9.90 metres wide, its enormous size and the high standard of its execution accentuate new design principles. So in various respects, this suq is a very interesting example of structural change in a traditional commercial centre.

aea6e497-0dd2-52bd-b31b-8f9ac8b8e29c.name: A photograph of the Arms Factory in Fez (*Dar al-makina*)
aea6e497-0dd2-52bd-b31b-8f9ac8b8e29c.description: A photograph depicting workers at the Arms Factory in Fez.
aea6e497-0dd2-52bd-b31b-8f9ac8b8e29c.holder: The Inspection of the Historic Monuments
aea6e497-0dd2-52bd-b31b-8f9ac8b8e29c.keywords: Industrialisation; industrialists; Italians in Morocco; social changes; work; labour; workers; machine; technical innovation; urban life; urban space; urbanisation; changes in warfare; protectorate; weapons; arms; armours; firearms; market

aecccc21-db80-57b6-bba8-ea4b65fba9be.name: The Iwan House
aecccc21-db80-57b6-bba8-ea4b65fba9be.description: The house is built around a vestibule, which is flanked on two sides by symmetrical living spaces and open on one end with a tall archway called an *iwan*, or an *'aqd* in the local dialect. It is after this archway that the vestibule is named. The *iwan* archway is usually north facing, for climactic reasons, and built in a broken or curved shape. The vestibule is sometimes T-shaped, with arms at the back leading to two adjacent rooms, or can simply be a wider room, thus becoming more of a central hall.
aecccc21-db80-57b6-bba8-ea4b65fba9be.author: Jeff El-Msanne, David Andos
aecccc21-db80-57b6-bba8-ea4b65fba9be.history: The architecture of the *iwan* was well suited to both its domestic and economic functions. When opened, it allowed the family to work and sit outside whilst remaining protected from the worst of the winter winds and summer sun. It also facilitated the movement of domestic animals, and the storage of produce and agricultural equipment. The house is built with *ramleh* of stone and limestone-marl from Ashrafiyyeh. Although mud was traditionally used, the walls nowadays are usually covered with reinforced concrete.
aecccc21-db80-57b6-bba8-ea4b65fba9be.keywords: Iwan; Architecture; Arc; Bow; Material; Typology

aed162cf-cef3-52e5-aa78-567138f64d2a.name: Bowl with stand
aed162cf-cef3-52e5-aa78-567138f64d2a.holder: Musée de la Céramique Sidi Kacem Jelizi
aed162cf-cef3-52e5-aa78-567138f64d2a.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
aed162cf-cef3-52e5-aa78-567138f64d2a.keywords: Floral motifs; winged motifs; cermaics from Nabeul
aed162cf-cef3-52e5-aa78-567138f64d2a.description2: This bowl with a bulging rim sits on a stand. The decoration is made of two layers of concentric patterns around a central circle, filled with winged motifs. These green and brown patterns are painted on a yellow background. Although this kind of bowl is usually used to serve couscous, in the town Nabeul, and particularly for the occasion of Islamic New Year, each child is presented with a *methred* bowl, filled with golden couscous, dried fruit, dates, a hard-boiled egg and sweets. This all surrounds a statuette made of sugar, moulded and coloured to resemble an animal (such as a rooster or a gazelle) or a figure, like a doll or cavalier.

aee0c11d-b05a-5082-9164-78ab982f4882.name: *A Greek lady of Smyrna*
aee0c11d-b05a-5082-9164-78ab982f4882.author: Delivorrias, Fotopoulos 1997, 503, fig. 888 (Elisabeth Karanopoulou)
aee0c11d-b05a-5082-9164-78ab982f4882.description2: The picture probably depicts a bride before being bedecked. Her outfit-one of the two customary types of urban bridal costume during the Ottoman period- consists of one or two pairs of pantaloons, a diaphanous selvedged chemise and a dress with tightly buttoned long sleeves and a sash worn low on the hips. Her overcoat is trimmed with fur, has wide pointed sleeves and the dress appears to have been hitched up, revealing the bottom of the pantaloons. Among the various testimonies bequeathed to us by the foreign artist-travelers who visited Greece in the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth centuries, the depictions of costumes are particularly important. The imaginative combination of the various garments and accessories that make up the Greek costume and the wealth of jewellery fascinated foreign travellers, who recorded them pictorially, often with a dubitable degree of accuracy.

en: Delivorrias, Angelos, and Fotopoulos, Dionisis, *Greece at the Benaki Museum*, Athens: Benaki Museum, 1997.

aee4fe30-32cf-540e-ab4a-7a1e2e832504.name: Grindstone
aee4fe30-32cf-540e-ab4a-7a1e2e832504.holder: National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography “Luigi Pigorini”
aee4fe30-32cf-540e-ab4a-7a1e2e832504.author: Marina Minozzi
aee4fe30-32cf-540e-ab4a-7a1e2e832504.keywords: Egyptomania; Gaetano Rosellini; university; collector; photograph; anthropology; palaeoethnology; material culture; Florence; Pisa; Egyptology; Nubia; languages; hieroglyph; William Matthew Flinders Petrie; Jacques de Morgan; David Randall-MacIver
aee4fe30-32cf-540e-ab4a-7a1e2e832504.description2: The stone grinder was used to pulverise colours or cosmetics. It represents an important relic for the history of the foundation of the Pigorini Museum. Its label, signed by Giglioli, attests that the object was discovered in Thebes by Ernesto Schiaparelli in January 1892 and then donated by him to Giglioli three months later. The grinder cannot be dated as its origins are unknown. As a result of the excavations by W. Petrie and J. De Morgan, who documented the existence of an era preceding the First dynasty, Luigi Pigorini decided to enlarge the Egyptian archaeological collection in the "Museo Preistorico Etnografico e Kircheriano" which he directed at the time. In 1878 he began to acquire important groups, but the main body of the collection was donated by David Randall-MacIver in 1901, from the excavations he carried out on the behalf of the Egypt Exploration Fund in the town of el-Amrah, Upper Egypt. In 1905 Ernesto Schiaparelli, director of the Egyptian Museum in Turin, offered for purchase the excavation of Hammamiye by the Italian Archaeological Mission in Egypt. The last main acquisition took place in 1913 when the Egyptian objects from Enrico Hillyer Giglioli’s collection entered the museum collection.

en: Cappozzo, M., “La collezione egizia del Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico ‘Luigi Pigorini’”, in *Bullettino di Paletnologia Italiana*, Roma, Istituto Poligrafico e Zecca dello Stato, (2005–2007), 96: 131–202, cat. 153.

aef7807d-0cef-5b06-ba3e-6be4aa40ba9c.name: Turkish woman
aef7807d-0cef-5b06-ba3e-6be4aa40ba9c.description2: The Zangaki brothers were a pair of photographers working in Egypt who sold "Orientalist" photos to Western tourists, allowing them to immortalise their trip to the "Orient". This photograph shows a young Turkish woman.

af2dcc82-957a-54c2-9a0f-e5e5ba86b4d3.name: Ottoman Clothing Album
af2dcc82-957a-54c2-9a0f-e5e5ba86b4d3.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
af2dcc82-957a-54c2-9a0f-e5e5ba86b4d3.dates: Late 19th century – beginning of the 20th century
af2dcc82-957a-54c2-9a0f-e5e5ba86b4d3.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph Ancient Istanbul; Pascal Sebah
af2dcc82-957a-54c2-9a0f-e5e5ba86b4d3.description2: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century. Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. Sébah opened a photography studio known as "El Chark " in Pera in 1857. The studio's most successful period started with the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873. Sébah formed a partnership with Joaillier Polycarpe in 1885. In 1899, the two partners bought Abdullah Frères's archives. For the Vienna Universal Exhibition in 1873, Pascal Sébah prepared *The Ottoman Clothing Album* to be exhibited at the Ottoman Stand.

af5dd515-10f6-573e-bba3-9212bf33f05f.name: Painting, *Royal Audience*
af5dd515-10f6-573e-bba3-9212bf33f05f.description: The painting depicts an audience with Sultan Muhammad IV ‘Abd al-Rahman in the city of Fez on 23 November 1868. The sultan, on horseback, receives the British Ambassador to Tangier, Sir John Drummond-Hay, who is seen accompanied by his staff and family.
af5dd515-10f6-573e-bba3-9212bf33f05f.keywords: John Drummond-Hay; British in Morocco;embassy; ambassador; Moroccan-British relations; international relations; diplomacy; diplomatic visits; travel; trade; trade agreement; Great Britain

af6de1c1-aac3-5b48-9d6c-1e99228574c4.name: Military personnel records
af6de1c1-aac3-5b48-9d6c-1e99228574c4.description:
The information sheets are part of the medical examination prior to the training of the new recruits. The newly enrolled were destined for the Protectorate which, due to the pressure of public opinion, refused the presence of Spaniards in that area.  
The records, along with a pair of photographs, gathered information on individuals’ social and professional backgrounds, as well as descriptive data and anthropometric values. Those values were used by the Medical Corps to determine the minimum size permitted to enter in the Army, but they were also important according to the existing racial theories in Spain.  
The sheets refer to these soldiers as “Moors” in a generic way, a colloquial and sometimes pejorative term of Latin etymology, which alludes to the population of the Maghreb with no regard to their origin, ethnicity or beliefs.

af86cd22-a9d6-5bda-a51c-2d290fb277bb.name: *Infantry-attack during the occupation-campaign in Bosnia-Herzegovina 1878*
af86cd22-a9d6-5bda-a51c-2d290fb277bb.holder: Austrian Military Museum / Institute of Military History
af86cd22-a9d6-5bda-a51c-2d290fb277bb.keywords: Bosnia; Austrian army; Ottoman army; Ottoman Balkans; war; warfare
af86cd22-a9d6-5bda-a51c-2d290fb277bb.description2: With an energetic stroke of the brush, Rudolph Konopa shows us an episode from the occupation campaign of the Austro-Hungarian Army in the Ottoman provinces of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1878. Konopa studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna and was a co-founder of the *Hagenbund* in 1900. Konopa received many awards, including the gold medal of the Vienna *Künstlerhaus*. Later during World War I, he became member of the so called *k.u.k. Kriegspressequartier* (art division of the ministry of War) and worked as a war painter on the eastern and southern fronts.

af9129f2-d726-50c7-86ec-2e0e2b8d352c.name: Astronomer Pierre Janssen (1824–1907) is carried in a ladder chair to the inauguration of the observatory on the Mont Blanc, at 4.807 m.

afd6e1d3-33ef-5931-b450-586de20009b5.name: Mrayjat Railway Station
afd6e1d3-33ef-5931-b450-586de20009b5.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
afd6e1d3-33ef-5931-b450-586de20009b5.history: The train line passing through this station went from Beirut to Damascus (Baramke) via Jamhur, 'Araya, 'Aley, Bhamdun, and 'Ayn Sawfar.
afd6e1d3-33ef-5931-b450-586de20009b5.keywords: Commerce; Train station; Railway; Transportation; Trading
afd6e1d3-33ef-5931-b450-586de20009b5.description2: This train station was not only built in the French style, but also operated in the same way as French railways, demonstrating the extent of French influence on architecture and infrastructure during this period: both passenger trains and freight trains, transporting goods and raw materials across land, served this line.

afd9edc1-f5ea-5e44-91d3-f71b09a91a1e.name: *Ibrahim Pasha*
afd9edc1-f5ea-5e44-91d3-f71b09a91a1e.keywords: Ruling Family; Rulers of Egypt; The Alawiyya Dynasty; Turks; The Ruling Elite
afd9edc1-f5ea-5e44-91d3-f71b09a91a1e.description2: Second ruler of the Muhammad 'Ali Dynasty, Ibrahim Pasha was the oldest of Muhammad 'Ali Pasha’s sons and his right hand in his conquests and projects. He came to Egypt with his brother Ahmad Tusun in 28 August 1805. He ruled Egypt for only two months.

afe3b20f-d59e-5494-b4ec-e5a4b9544ad9.name: Zeybek Folk Dance
afe3b20f-d59e-5494-b4ec-e5a4b9544ad9.description2: Zeybek is a folk dance from Western Anatolia. It is done either by one or several dancers moving in a circle. Zeybek represents the protector. The dancer keeps his arms upright on the shoulder level while sometimes they are curled from elbow. He moves slowly with long steps. From time to time he kneels to touch his knee down.

aff0f573-5e91-5646-94a2-26bd51ba0e14.name: *Interior of a Harem*
aff0f573-5e91-5646-94a2-26bd51ba0e14.description: This painting was made around 1863 when the author travelled to Morocco with Mariano Fortuny. The reason for his travel was to paint the characters and picturesque garments as the way of life of the people from Morocco. The influence his experiences had on his works can be found in his paintings and drawings. During his travels he bought exotic artworks, such as Egyptian sarcophagi. Harem and markets are considered a genre painting in Orientalism.
aff0f573-5e91-5646-94a2-26bd51ba0e14.author: Carolina Miguel Arroyo
aff0f573-5e91-5646-94a2-26bd51ba0e14.keywords: North Africa; Orientalism; Travelling; Harem; Women

aff1ae5a-f832-5831-b8c0-8ad91d5e93ec.name: Inkstand
aff1ae5a-f832-5831-b8c0-8ad91d5e93ec.keywords: Arts and Crafts; Daily utilitarian ware; Portugal; Vista Alegre; Factory
aff1ae5a-f832-5831-b8c0-8ad91d5e93ec.description2: Inskstandish shaped like a brigantine, representing young triton blowing on a conch trumpet. Ink wells, lids and edges decorated with flowers in polychrome. Base of the inkstand is rested on waves, painted in shades of green.  The inkstandish reflects the taste for nautical representations, evoking the national maritime glory, while it introduces delicate floral motifs, in the romantic style of that epoch. Painted by Victor Rousseau, master of painting in the Vista Alegre Porcelain Factory, this object is an example of the early decorative tendencies, distinguishable by the virtuosity of the drawings, intricate forms and artistic experimentation.

en: Arez, Ilda, *et al.*, *Vista Alegre Porcelanas*, Lisbon: Inapa, 1989.
Henriques, Paulo, “Ciclos de Modernidade” in Mântua, Ana Anjos (ed), *Cerâmica Portuguesa do século XVI ao século XX*, Geneva: Musée Ariana, 2004.

b0034e9d-b0b0-5bbc-a3c7-5d26a2e4d496.name: Textile
b0034e9d-b0b0-5bbc-a3c7-5d26a2e4d496.description: Cotton textile made in twill weave. The complete surface is decorated, in different colours, with the writing decoration in silver and white lines.

b01b920c-bd76-5e6a-b3c9-4e331c550bdd.name: Karagöz and Hacivat Shadow Play
b01b920c-bd76-5e6a-b3c9-4e331c550bdd.description2: Shadow play consists of solid figures being shown and moved behind a semi-transparent screen. The characters of Hacivat and Karagöz plays reflect the multi-ethnic makeup of the Ottoman Empire. They are represented with a high level of detail through their figures, attitudes, dances, etc. Shadow play received its basic character in the 17th century and developed further in the following centuries, eventually becoming one of the most popular traditional forms of entertainment among Turks. It was performed by a single artist that is called a *hayali* (imaginary person) or *hayalbaz*. One of the main characteristics of shadow play is that the *hayali* changes his voice and manner of speaking depending on the character he was animating.

b08652d5-bffa-5858-a142-61103d91cf12.name: *Khayali* necklace and earrings
b08652d5-bffa-5858-a142-61103d91cf12.holder: Musée des Arts et Traditions Populaires
b08652d5-bffa-5858-a142-61103d91cf12.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
b08652d5-bffa-5858-a142-61103d91cf12.description2: Although it was originally used in Tunis as both a necklace and head jewellery (like a diadem), the *khayali* was worn in other Tunisian towns simply as a necklace. It consists of a very thin gold chain with rose-encrusted diamonds pendants. The *khayali* is made of 9-carat gold and inspired by the European style. The *sboulitat* earrings are also made of 9-carat gold and encrusted with roses.

b09ea51a-72ba-5a0c-8a5d-88c708d9a1fa.name: Women going about their daily life
b09ea51a-72ba-5a0c-8a5d-88c708d9a1fa.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
b09ea51a-72ba-5a0c-8a5d-88c708d9a1fa.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
b09ea51a-72ba-5a0c-8a5d-88c708d9a1fa.description2: In the eary 20th century the Tunisian woman, like her counterparts around the world, led a difficult life of hard work and exclusion from public life which was considered a man's world. Although it is important to take into account the variety of women's circumstances and experiences, depending on their background, it was nonetheless rare for a Tunisian woman at this time to have access to religious sciences, Arabic literature and even less so to the physical and mathematical sciences. The era of the great female poets, litterateurs and arts advocates in Kairouan had long passed. However a debate surrounding women's education was opening up in Tunisia, and particularly in Egypt, which presented women's education as a essential to the emancipation of society.
